Reference-to-video → character reference attach → shot prompt paste → aspect ratio select → Generate.
2-3 takes → best (face + hands sahi).
Connect: last frame SAVE → prompt bar 'Start/End' → Start frame set → next shot prompt → Generate.
Face gadbad → Ingredients me [last frame + character sheet] + upar wali face-consistency line.

videos.title: Camera Movement
videos.description:
Learn how camera direction can shape the mood and storytelling of an AI-generated shot. This lesson introduces eight camera techniques: slow push-in, pull-out, handheld, static or locked camera, orbit or arc, tracking, pan, and tilt. You will explore when to use each approach, from highlighting emotion with a slow push-in to creating tension with handheld movement or following a character with a tracking shot.
You will also learn the difference between a horizontal pan and a vertical tilt, along with how reveals and stillness can support a scene. The lesson’s central prompting rule is to keep each shot focused on one camera movement rather than combining multiple directions that may produce inconsistent results.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
English translation of the supplied Lesson 07 notesLESSON 07  |  1
LESSON 07 / 08
Camera Movement (8 Types)
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to choose a camera movement that suits a shot's emotion or
action and include it in a Flow prompt. The course rule is: one movement per shot.
Write the movement into your prompt
Camera movement is not just a matter of memorising names. The source connects each movement with a
purpose: emotion, reveal, tension, stillness, drama or a journey. When planning a shot, think about its
purpose first, then choose a relevant movement.
1. Slow push-in. For emotion and close-ups. The camera slowly moves closer to the character, focusing
attention on the emotional moment. Practice cue: A slow push-in towards the young man's face as he
listens to the old voice note.
2. Pull-out. For reveals, endings and loneliness. The camera moves away from the character and reveals
the surrounding scene. Practice cue: Pull out from the character at the ending to show him sitting alone in
the room.
3. Handheld. For a raw, tense or panicked feeling. This choice relates to a tense treatment rather than
calm stillness. Practice cue: Specify handheld camera treatment in the prompt for a moment when the
character is panicking.
4. Static / locked. For stillness and loneliness. The camera stays fixed; it is not given a pan or tracking
direction. Practice cue: The young man sits quietly while the camera remains locked in one position.
5. Orbit / arc. For a dramatic scene or a hero moment. The camera moves around the character. Practice
cue: Choose an orbit or arc around the subject to give a hero moment a dramatic treatment.
6. Tracking. For walking and journeys. The camera's movement is connected to the character's walking.
Practice cue: Write tracking in the camera instruction for a shot that follows the character's walking
journey.
7. Pan. For a left-to-right or right-to-left reveal. The camera stays in one place and turns only left or right.
The direction is horizontal. Practice cue: Reveal the room from left to right without changing the camera's
position.
8. Tilt. For revealing height or detail. The camera stays in one place and turns up or down. Its direction
distinguishes it from a pan. Practice cue: Use an upward tilt to reveal a high place.
Key rule and revision practice
Specify only one movement per shot. The source links multiple movements with a risk of glitches. Added
practice: Write one camera choice beside each prepared shot and explain your reason, such as a slow
push-in for an emotional moment or tracking for walking.
Self-check: What is the difference between a pan and a tilt? When would you use a static camera? Does each shot
contain only one camera-movement instruction?
videos.examplePrompt:
Lesson 7 — Camera Movement words
slow push-in — emotion, close-up
slow pull-out — reveal, ending, akelapan
handheld, strong shake — raw, tense, panic
static locked camera — stillness, akelapan
camera orbits around — dramatic, hero moment
tracking shot, follow — walking, journey
slow horizontal pan (stays fixed, only rotates, NO push-in) — left-right reveal
slow tilt up (stays fixed, only rotates, NO push-in/zoom) — height/detail reveal
Rule: ek shot me ek hi movement. Handheld weak aaye to: 'STRONG handheld, visibly shaking, run-and-gun, she walks'.

videos.title: Shot Types / Framing
videos.description:
Understand how framing changes what the audience sees and how they experience a scene. This lesson introduces six essential shot types: wide, medium, close-up, extreme close-up, point-of-view, and over-the-shoulder. You will learn how each framing choice serves a different purpose, from establishing the environment with a wide shot to highlighting emotion with a close-up.
The lesson also explores how extreme close-ups draw attention to details, point-of-view shots show a scene through a character’s eyes, and over-the-shoulder framing supports conversations. By understanding how much of the subject and surroundings to include, you will be better prepared to choose shots that match your story’s emotional intent. The central idea is simple: changing the framing changes the feeling.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
English translation of the supplied Lesson 08 notesLESSON 08  |  1
LESSON 08 / 08
Shot Types / Framing (6 Types)
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to decide how much to show in a shot: the environment, a
character, a face, a detail, someone's viewpoint or a view from behind a shoulder.
Framing means deciding how much to show
Framing determines what the audience sees in a shot and how much is visible. The source's key rule is:
change the framing, and the feeling changes. Choose a shot type to suit the emotion and the scene's
purpose, not just its name.
1. Wide. For showing the entire scene and environment. The source connects this framing with
establishing the scene and conveying loneliness. Wide framing fits when you need to show the character
together with the surrounding space.
2. Medium. Waist-up framing for ordinary conversation. The source describes this as the default shot
type. Remember it in the context of showing a character in normal conversation; it differs from wide
framing, which shows the whole environment.
3. Close-up. For the face and emotion. This framing focuses attention on the face. When the character's
feelings are the shot's main focus, the source maps the close-up to that purpose.
4. Extreme close-up. For an eye, a hand or another specific detail. The source links this framing with
tension. A close-up may focus on the face; the main idea of an extreme close-up is to isolate and highlight
a small detail.
5. POV. For showing the scene through a character's eyes. The source uses the word "immersive":
presenting the view as someone's perspective. Think of this as choosing the character's viewpoint rather
than looking at the character from outside.
6. Over-the-shoulder. A view from behind a shoulder, especially for a conversation between two people.
The key cue is the position behind the shoulder. The source uses this framing in the context of
conversation.
Understand movement and framing separately
In Lesson 7, you chose camera movement; here, you decide how much to show in the shot. Revision
example: Specifying close-up framing with a slow push-in makes two separate choices: framing and
movement. The one-movement rule still applies.
Practice example
For the old voice-note story, a practice exercise could be to choose a wide shot for the room and
character, a close-up for his emotional face and an extreme close-up for a detail of his hand. This is not the
shot list of the film demonstrated in the source.
Revision practice
Choose one framing type for each of your prepared shots. Write the reason beside it: environment,
conversation, emotion, detail or viewpoint. This added exercise helps you revise the source's six framing
types.
Self-check: What is the difference between a close-up and an extreme close-up? Does your shot need to emphasise
the environment or the emotion on the character's face?

videos.title: Emotion & Expression
videos.description: Learn how to communicate believable emotions through precise, expression-based prompts. This lesson explores the facial cues associated with happiness, sadness, crying, anger, fear, and surprise, helping you move beyond general instructions such as “make the character sad.” Discover how details in the eyes, eyebrows, mouth, and facial tension communicate the intended feeling. The lesson also emphasises preserving the same character identity across close-ups and changing expressions. By the end, you will understand how to describe emotions more clearly while keeping your character visually consistent.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 09LESSON 09  |  1
LESSON 09 / 15
Emotion & Expression
Learn to describe visible emotional cues clearly while keeping the same character identity in every
close-up.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
Describe the expression, not just the emotion
The central lesson is to replace a vague emotion word with specific facial details. Instead of writing only
"sad", describe what the eyes, mouth and face are doing. The supplied notes connect more detailed
expression cues with a more convincing feeling. The prompt should make the intended expression visible,
rather than leaving it as an abstract label.
Six emotions and their visible cues
Happiness: Use a soft, genuine smile, warm eyes and a slight laugh. These cues describe a gentle, happy
expression rather than simply naming the feeling.
Sadness: Describe eyes welling with tears, a downturned mouth and a heavy look. Keep these details
together when you want the face to communicate sadness.
Crying: Describe tears welling and falling, trembling lips and red eyes. The notes distinguish crying from
sadness through these more explicit signs, especially the falling tears and trembling lips.
Anger: Use a furrowed brow, a clenched jaw and an intense stare. The brow, jaw and gaze are the specific
parts of the expression highlighted in this lesson.
Fear: Describe wide eyes, a tense face and slight trembling. In the lesson, the tension and trembling
accompany the wide-eyed expression.
Surprise: Use raised eyebrows, an open mouth and wide eyes. Compare this combination with fear: wide
eyes appear in both, but the other details are different.
Keep the face consistent
The source specifically requires the exact same face in a close-up. A change of expression should not
become a change of character. Check identity and emotion separately: first confirm that it is still the same
person, then check whether the requested expression is visible. "Face lock" here describes the required
result; this lesson does not name a dedicated interface control.
Practice example - added study aid
Vague: "The character is sad." Detailed: "Close-up of the same character, eyes welling with tears, a
downturned mouth and a heavy look; preserve the exact same face." This example combines the lesson's
sadness cues with its close-up identity rule.
Practice task - added study aid
Write one expression prompt for sadness and another for crying, using the same character. Underline the
cues that differ. When reviewing the results, compare both the emotional details and the character's face.
Self-check: Can you show the emotion through specific facial details? Is the character still recognisably the same
person in the close-up?

Udaasi: welling eyes, downturned mouth, heavy look
Rona: tears welling and falling, trembling lips, red eyes

Hairaani: raised eyebrows, mouth open, wide eyes
Close-up me: 'EXACT same face as reference, DO NOT change/morph the face'.

videos.title: Lighting & Mood
videos.description: Explore how lighting supports the emotional direction of a scene and shapes its atmosphere. This lesson introduces six lighting treatments: warm soft light, cold blue light, golden-hour lighting, dim night lighting, soft diffused light, and hard dramatic light with strong shadows. Understand how the course uses these treatments to communicate feelings such as comfort, loneliness, hope, mystery, calmness, and intensity. Rather than choosing lighting only for its visual appeal, learn to connect it to the story’s intended emotion and write lighting instructions that support that creative decision.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 10LESSON 10  |  1
LESSON 10 / 15
Lighting & Mood
Choose lighting that supports the scene's intended emotion, using the six lighting treatments
introduced in the lesson.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
Start with the scene's feeling
The main rule is to match the light to the emotion of the scene. Decide whether the moment should feel
happy, lonely, hopeful, mysterious, calm or intense, then choose the lighting description that matches it.
The six options below preserve the emotional associations in the supplied lesson; they are a guide for this
course, not a claim that a lighting style has only one possible meaning.
Six lighting treatments
Warm soft light: The lesson links this with a cosy atmosphere, happiness and home. Use both words in the
description: "warm" expresses the colour treatment, while "soft" is part of the lighting quality requested in
the notes.
Cold blue light: Associated with sadness, loneliness and tension. Select this treatment when those feelings
are the intended focus, rather than choosing blue simply as an unrelated visual effect.
Golden hour: Linked with beauty, hope and romance. The lesson uses this as an emotional lighting choice.
It does not provide exact time-of-day instructions, exposure values or a technical lighting setup.
Dim, low night light: Associated with tension, mystery and drama. Preserve the night-time and dim-light
description when applying this option; those qualities are part of the supplied cue.
Soft diffused light: Linked with a calm, gentle and flattering appearance. This option emphasises a softer
emotional treatment rather than the intensity highlighted by hard dramatic light.
Hard dramatic light with strong shadows: Used for an intense feeling. Strong shadows are an explicit part
of this instruction, so include them rather than writing only the broad word "dramatic".
Make the choice intentional
Read the emotion and lighting instruction together. A useful application of the lesson is to complete the
sentence: "This scene should feel ___, so I am choosing ___." This connects the visual decision to the story.
When comparing two results, focus on whether the selected treatment supports the feeling you planned.
Practice example - added study aid
For a lonely moment, write a lighting instruction using cold blue light. For a hopeful version of the same
moment, try golden-hour lighting. These are practice applications of the source's mood pairings, not
descriptions of a demonstrated scene.
Practice task - added study aid
Choose three moments from your own film. Write the intended emotion beside each one, then select a
lighting treatment from this page. Explain the match in one sentence before generating the shot.
Self-check: What should the audience feel? Which lighting option supports it? Have you included the specific
lighting qualities named in the lesson?

"golden hour light" — khoobsurat / romantic

"soft diffused light" — calm / flattering
"hard dramatic light, strong shadows" — intense

videos.title: Realism Tricks
videos.description: Develop a more natural, candid visual style by using specific details instead of relying on broad quality labels. This lesson introduces realism cues such as visible skin texture, pores, fine facial hair, natural light, neutral colours, and handheld movement. It also examines the features that work against the course’s intended aesthetic, including waxy skin, excessive smoothing, beauty filters, heavy colour grading, and unwanted slow motion. Learn to recognise these issues in generated shots and refine your prompts with clearer descriptions of texture, lighting, colour, and movement.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 11LESSON 11  |  1
LESSON 11 / 15
Realism Tricks
Build the raw, candid look taught in the course through visible skin texture, natural light, neutral colours
and restrained styling.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
The lesson's realism principle
The source contrasts a slightly imperfect, natural-looking image with an over-perfect, artificial-looking
result. Its practical emphasis is on describing observable details rather than repeating impressive-sounding
quality words. Apply these notes to the raw, candid style being taught here; the aim is not to make every
film look highly polished.
What to include in the prompt
A raw, candid iPhone look: This is the visual description used in the notes. Keep the request focused on a
candid appearance rather than an over-styled image. The source does not specify a camera model, a
recording format or a technical RAW-file workflow.
Real skin texture: Ask for visible pores and peach fuzz, meaning fine facial hair. These are the concrete
skin details supplied by the lesson. Pair them with "not smoothed" and "no filter" so the requested
appearance remains natural rather than cosmetically perfected.
Natural light and neutral colours: Both are included in the recommended realism cues. Use them together
when following this lesson's look instead of combining the prompt with a request for heavy colour
grading.
Handheld shake: The notes include this as part of the candid treatment. It is a movement cue, separate
from the skin, lighting and colour instructions. The source does not specify a shake amount or a numerical
camera setting.
What to avoid for this treatment
Avoid repeatedly adding "8K" or "ultra" in place of descriptive detail. The source also warns against waxy
or plastic-looking skin, beauty filters, heavy grading, slow motion and an over-perfect appearance. These
are the contrasts to the natural texture, ordinary speed and restrained styling sought in the course.
The useful distinction is between naming a visible quality and adding a broad label. "Visible pores, natural
light, no skin smoothing" describes the requested look more directly than a string of quality adjectives.
Practice prompt - added study aid
"Raw, candid iPhone look; real skin with visible pores and peach fuzz; natural light, neutral colours and
handheld shake; no skin smoothing, beauty filter, heavy grading or slow motion." This practice prompt
assembles the source's own realism cues; it is not a guaranteed generation result.
Practice task - added study aid
Review one generated shot against four areas: skin texture, lighting, colour treatment and movement.
Note any waxy skin, strong filtering or unwanted slow motion. Rewrite the relevant part of the prompt
using the lesson's concrete cues.
Self-check: Does the image preserve natural texture? Do the lighting and colours match the candid look? Have
quality labels replaced useful detail?

DON'T — mat likho

videos.title: B-roll & Cutaways
videos.description: Discover how supporting shots contribute to a story beyond its main action. This lesson introduces five categories of B-roll and cutaways: objects and details, hands and actions, establishing shots, textures and atmosphere, and character reactions. Explore how these shots can provide context, show activity, establish a location, communicate emotion, or conceal an edit. Following the course’s practice of planning one or two supporting shots between main shots, you will learn to select inserts with a clear storytelling purpose rather than adding unrelated visuals simply to fill space.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 12LESSON 12  |  1
LESSON 12 / 15
B-roll & Cutaways
Plan supporting shots that add context, show activity, establish a location, build mood or reveal a
reaction between main shots.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
Give each supporting shot a purpose
This lesson groups B-roll and cutaways by the job they perform around the main shots. A supporting shot
may show an object, an action, the location, an atmospheric detail or a reaction. Choose the insert
according to what the sequence needs, rather than adding an unrelated image simply to fill space.
Five types introduced in the lesson
Object or detail: A cup or phone can provide context and help fill a gap between main shots. Here the
focus is the item itself. Select a detail that belongs to the scene so the cutaway remains connected to the
surrounding material.
Hands or action: Typing and pouring are the source's examples. These inserts show an activity taking
place. Compared with an object-only shot, the important element is what the hands are doing, not just
which item appears.
Establishing shot: A wide view of the location sets the scene. Its role is to show the place in which the
main action happens. This is the location-focused option in the lesson's list.
Texture or mood: Rain, steam and pages are examples of details used to create a feeling. Their purpose in
this lesson is atmospheric: the insert contributes to the mood of the sequence.
Reaction: A cutaway to a face or the eyes highlights emotion and can help hide an edit. The emphasis is on
the response, rather than on the object, activity or setting that the other categories show.
Placement between main shots
The source gives a course rule of placing one or two B-roll shots between main shots. Use that instruction
while practising this workflow, and identify the purpose of each insert. The notes do not specify exact
shot lengths, transition settings or a timing formula.
Before placing an insert, name its function: context, activity, location, atmosphere or reaction. This makes
it easier to explain why it belongs between the two main shots. An image that looks attractive but has no
clear relationship to the sequence does not demonstrate the purpose-based approach taught here.
Practice sequence - added study aid
Between two main shots of a character, try a phone-detail insert for context and a close view of the
character's eyes for a reaction. Alternatively, use a pouring action to show activity. These examples apply
the categories; they are not the original film's shot list.
Practice task - added study aid
Choose two adjacent main shots from your film. Plan one or two inserts and label each with its category
and purpose. Check that both inserts belong to the same scene or clearly support its feeling.
Self-check: What does each insert contribute? Is it showing an object, an action, a place, a mood or a reaction? Why
is it placed here?
videos.examplePrompt:
Lesson 12 — B-roll shot prompts
Object: close-up of a cup / phone / object on a table, shallow focus, natural light
Hands: close-up of hands typing / pouring / holding, natural movement
Establishing: wide shot of the location (room/street/cafe)
Texture: rain on a window / pages flipping / steam rising, close-up
Reaction: a subtle face/eyes reaction (EXACT same face as reference)

videos.title: Editing
videos.description: Bring your generated material together through a practical breakdown of an existing film’s CapCut project. This lesson walks through the complete timeline, arranging clips in Hook, Build, Twist, and End order, and placing sound at the appropriate story moments. Explore the role of office ambience, phone rings, busy tones, voicemail, and light music within the sequence. The emphasis is on straightforward assembly and purposeful organisation rather than complicated effects. By the end, you will understand how to arrange your clips and sound into a clear sequence that follows your planned story.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 13LESSON 13  |  1
LESSON 13 / 15
Editing (CapCut Breakdown)
Understand the four-part editing walkthrough: review the timeline, arrange the story, place suitable
sound and keep the assembly simple.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
Study the film as an organised timeline
The lesson is presented as a breakdown of an existing film's CapCut project. Its focus is not a long list of
effects, but how video and sound are arranged to form the film. The supplied outline divides this
demonstration into four parts. Use those parts as a map when studying or assembling your own edit.
1. Review the complete timeline
Begin with the whole timeline rather than treating each clip as an isolated result. The source names a
complete timeline overview as the first part of the demonstration. For revision, identify the overall
sequence and where its different pieces belong. The supplied notes do not reproduce the project or
provide its exact timestamps.
2. Put clips in story order
Arrange the clips according to Hook, Build, Twist and End. This is the story order explicitly given in the
lesson. Match each clip to its planned story role, then check that the sequence follows those four parts.
The goal is to assemble the selected material into the intended story, not merely place files in an arbitrary
order.
3. Put the right sound in the right place
The sound examples listed are office ambience, a phone ring, a busy tone, voicemail and light music. The
lesson's emphasis is on placing the appropriate sound at the appropriate moment. Relate each sound to
the event or atmosphere it accompanies, rather than treating every sound as interchangeable background
audio.
The source does not include precise audio positions, volume levels or mixing controls. Keep those details
separate from what the outline actually teaches: the relationship between the story moment and the
selected sound.
4. Keep the assembly simple
The final point highlights how straightforward the basic edit can be: put the videos on the timeline and
arrange them in sequence. Follow this core task before assuming the lesson requires an elaborate effect
stack. The notes do not provide transition presets, export settings or a detailed button-by-button editing
guide.
Practice task - added study aid
Using your own clips, write a short list in Hook, Build, Twist and End order. Add a sound note beside any
moment that needs one of the types discussed above. Assemble that sequence in CapCut, then review the
whole timeline and compare it with your written plan.
For a second review, explain why each clip and sound is in its chosen position. This checks the organising
principles from the lesson without inventing details from the demonstrated project.
Self-check: Does the timeline follow the planned story order? Does each sound belong to its moment? Is the basic
sequence complete and understandable?

Har clip ka pehla ~0.5 sec trim
Sound sahi jagah: ambience, phone ring, busy tone, voicemail; music 20-30% (low); emotional peak par silence

videos.title: Common Mistakes + Pro Tips
videos.description: Review common AI filmmaking problems and the course’s suggested approaches to addressing them. This final lesson covers changing character faces, hand glitches, artificial-looking skin, blurred sides, unwanted yellow colour casts, slow movement, and distorted text. Revisit the use of character references, Start-frame, and Ingredients, along with simpler actions, clearer visual descriptions, and adding text in CapCut rather than generating it in Flow. Learn to identify the specific issue, apply a relevant adjustment, and review the result instead of expecting one prompt to solve everything. The course concludes by encouraging you to apply the complete workflow to your first film.
videos.notes:
skillomate
AI FILMMAKING  /  ENGLISH STUDENT NOTES
Source: AI_Filmmaking_Notes_L9-15.docx, Lesson 15LESSON 15  |  1
LESSON 15 / 15
Common Mistakes + Pro Tips
Recognise the seven problems listed in the finale and connect each one with its corresponding course
troubleshooting suggestion.
Expanded from the supplied lesson outline. Labelled practice sections and self-checks are added study aids.
Identify the problem before choosing a fix
The finale pairs common generation problems with short corrective suggestions. Use the pairs below as a
revision checklist. A changing face, extra hands and broken text are different problems; the lesson does
not propose one universal prompt that fixes everything.
Seven problem-and-response pairs
1. The face changes: Use the character reference, Start-frame and Ingredients. These are the three
resources named in the source for identity consistency. The aim is to retain the same person across shots,
rather than accepting a different face in each clip.
2. Glitches or extra hands appear: Keep one action per clip and include the instruction "five fingers". This
preserves the lesson's simple-action approach and its explicit hand cue. Treat the wording as a
troubleshooting suggestion, not a guarantee that every anatomy error will disappear.
3. The result looks artificial: Ask for real skin and a candid look, and remove repeated "8K ultra" wording.
This revisits the realism lesson: use visible, natural-looking details rather than relying on broad quality
labels.
4. A violation warning appears: The notes advise removing falls, hits, revealing content or spoken-price
content. They do not explain these categories or cite a platform policy. Preserve this as a course-specific
troubleshooting note, not a verified list of prohibited content or a guaranteed fix.
5. The sides are blurred: Use a landscape reference, as the source recommends. Check the reference
orientation when reviewing this issue. The notes do not give exact dimensions, an aspect-ratio value or a
technical explanation for the blur.
6. The result is too yellow or too slow: Use cool-neutral colour, normal speed and a raw iPhone look.
These are the three cues supplied for this problem. Check both colour and motion, since the lesson groups
an unwanted warm cast and unwanted slow movement together.
7. Text is distorted: Add the text in CapCut rather than generating it in Flow. This separates the written
overlay from the generated shot. The source does not specify a particular text style, font or caption
preset.
Review exercise - added study aid
Watch your selected clips and note any of the seven issues above. Match each issue to its corresponding
suggestion before revising the prompt, changing the reference or moving the text work into the editor.
Recheck the result rather than assuming the first adjustment solved it.
Finale: make your first film
The source closes by asking you to create your first film. Apply the course's generation and editing
workflow, using this checklist to review the individual clips as you bring them together.
Self-check: Which issue are you correcting? Does the proposed change match it? Have you checked the new result
before using it in your film?

USE THIS IMAGE [saved last frame] AS THE FIRST FRAME AND TO KEEP THE FACE CONSISTENT THIS IS THE CHARACTER SHEET [reference]. [character description]. [location]. [shot action]. realistic, 9:16, no on-screen text, no watermark, NO background music.

Violate → fall/hit/revealing/spoken-price hatao (price text pe)
Sides blurred (16:9) → LANDSCAPE 16:9 reference use karo
Yellow/slow → 'cool-neutral white balance, normal real-time speed, raw iPhone'
Text glitch → Flow me text nahi, CapCut me add

Lesson 06: Photo to Product Video
Learning Objective
Animate product photographs with controlled cinematic movement
Preparation and Context
Select a good product photograph from the earlier lessons.
Step-by-Step Process
In Google Flow choose Video and Ingredients and add the photo. The source demonstrates 16:9, 720p,
six seconds and Omni 1.1 Flash. Make separate clips using one movement each: slow push-in, gentle
camera arc or light sweep with the camera still.

Keep the product stationary and inspect its details frame by frame. Add music later in editing rather
than generation.
Example AI Prompt
Keep the product exactly the same as the source image. Make one slow camera push-in over six
seconds. The product remains still, with no morphing, changed lettering or altered geometry.

Combining spinning, flying and disassembly causes morphing. Small text can shift during movement;
use slower motion and generate multiple versions.

Lesson 07: UGC-Style Video
Learning Objective
Produce a natural phone-camera-style promotional clip
Preparation and Context

courses.title: AI Local Business Ads
courses.description:
AI Local Business Ads
Professional course description
AI Local Business Ads is a practical, beginner-friendly course designed to help small business owners and
aspiring local content creators produce honest, effective marketing assets using accessible AI tools. Through
ten focused lessons, learners move from understanding a business and its customers to creating polished
shop and menu photography, offer and festival posters, short promotional videos, Hindi voiceover reels and
manageable publishing plans.
The course demonstrates how ChatGPT supports business briefs, writing and planning; how Google Flow can
assist with image and video creation; how CapCut brings clips together; and how ElevenLabs can provide an
optional text-to-speech workflow. It also introduces the fundamentals of offering this work as a service to
neighborhood businesses.
What learners will gain
Build a reusable business brief with customer segments, advertising angles and a content calendar.
Improve real shop, food and product photos while preserving their authentic appearance.
Create promotional posters using exact, approved wording and verified prices.
Produce short vertical reels and natural Hindi voiceovers.
Prepare platform-specific content for Instagram, WhatsApp and Google Business Profile.
Package creative services, collect client requirements and manage approvals.
Who this course is for
Owners of cafes, salons, bakeries, neighborhood stores and other local businesses.
Beginners interested in creating AI-assisted marketing content for nearby shops.
Content creators seeking a practical, ethical workflow for small-business clients.

courses.title: AI Cartoon Series
courses.description:
Learn how to create an original children’s cartoon series using ChatGPT, Google Flow and CapCut. This practical course takes you from your first idea to a complete animated episode, using Golu and Chiku as a running example.

You will develop distinctive characters, create reusable reference sheets and locations, write engaging stories for young audiences, and organise them into simple scenes. Step-by-step lessons explain how to generate start frames, animate short clips, plan character voices and maintain continuity across an episode. You will also produce an original rhyme video and learn practical ways to correct common visual and audio issues.

The course concludes with editing, thumbnail design, publishing preparation and a plan for future episodes. Designed for parents, teachers and aspiring creators, it requires no prior drawing or animation experience and focuses on building a clear, repeatable production workflow.

videos.title: FOUNDATIONS
videos.description: Discover the complete workflow for creating an original AI cartoon series for children. Explore how ChatGPT, Google Flow and CapCut support character development, scene production and editing. Using Golu and Chiku as the running example, you will define your audience, understand the course projects and prepare a clear plan for your own series.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 01  /  FOUNDATIONS
Course Introduction and Production
Workflow
Understand how a simple idea becomes a complete AI cartoon episode.
What this course helps you create
This course introduces a practical process for making original animated stories and rhymes for
children. The running example is Golu and Chiku: a six-year-old boy and his pet squirrel. Their
first story, Chiku and the Missing Laddoo, provides a shared project that develops across the
lessons. The focus is learning a repeatable production method, from planning characters to
preparing a finished episode.
The course is intended for parents, teachers and creators who want to make children's content.
Prior drawing or animation experience is not required. You still make the creative decisions:
choose the audience, approve the story, check the generated visuals and decide whether the
finished video communicates clearly.
Understand the role of each tool
- ChatGPT helps develop character descriptions, image and video prompts, stories, scene tables,
production sheets and publishing text. Review its suggestions before using them.
- Google Flow creates the visual assets and short animated clips. The course demonstrates Nano
Banana Pro for images and Frames or Ingredients workflows for video generation.
- CapCut brings the approved clips together. It is used for arranging scenes, adding a title card,
balancing music beneath dialogue and exporting the finished video.
Follow the production sequence
Begin with character reference sheets, then create three reusable locations. Write a short story
and divide it into scenes. Produce a clear starting image for each scene before animating it. Add
voice instructions, check continuity, assemble the clips, and prepare the thumbnail and
publishing information.
The demonstration episode uses eight eight-second scenes, giving 64 seconds of scene footage
before editing adjustments or a separate title card. The rhyme project uses four eight-second
clips, giving 32 seconds. These small projects let you practise the full workflow without
managing a long film.
The central production principle
Establish the design before animation
Reuse approved character sheets, the same Master Style line and the correct location
reference. These provide a consistent visual starting point; inspect every result because
prompts and references do not guarantee a perfect match.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 4; All Prompts p. 1; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-2.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 01  /  PLAN YOUR FIRST SERIES
Course Introduction and Production Workflow
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Decide who you are creating for
Choose a specific intended audience within the course example of children aged three to eight.
This choice guides vocabulary, the number of events in a story, the pace of delivery and how
clearly the lesson or moral must be shown. A young viewer should be able to follow the central
problem without needing an explanation outside the video.
Write a short series brief before requesting prompts. Include the working series name, intended
age group, two original main characters, the relationship between them and the kind of stories
you want to tell. Keep the first concept manageable: one small problem, familiar surroundings
and a warm resolution.
Prepare a reusable project record
1. Keep the context together. Use one working ChatGPT conversation when practical, and
save the approved series brief separately. If you start a new conversation, provide that brief and
the relevant references again.
2. Organise approved assets. Create clearly named folders for character sheets, locations,
scripts, scene images, video clips and final exports. Separate experiments from approved
designs.
3. Record successful decisions. Save the exact Master Style line, approved prompts and a
note of which references produced each accepted result. Course tool names and menus may
differ from your account.
Avoid common beginner mistakes
Generating random clips before deciding on the characters often produces material that does
not belong in the same series. Build the visual references first. Asking for an entire busy story in
one short clip also makes the action difficult to control; later lessons divide the story into one
clear action per scene.
Do not judge success only by how attractive one image looks. Ask whether the same character,
setting and story can be recognised across the complete sequence. A clear, simple episode is a
useful first milestone.
Practice task and completion check
Write a short brief for your own series. Name your audience, introduce two original characters,
describe their relationship and suggest one everyday problem for a first episode. Save the brief
for Lesson 02.
- Can you explain what each of the three tools contributes?
- Can you list the main stages from character design to publishing?
- Is your first idea small enough to tell through a short sequence of simple scenes?
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 4; All Prompts p. 1; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-2.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: BUILD THE CHARACTER FOUNDATION
videos.description: Learn to turn an original character idea into a clear design brief and reusable reference sheet. Define personality, appearance, clothing and colours, then generate matching views and expressions with a fixed Master Style line. You will also test both characters together and review their consistency before using them in future scenes.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 02  /  BUILD THE CHARACTER FOUNDATION
Designing Characters and Reference
Sheets
Create recognisable characters and a visual reference you can reuse.
Define the character before generating images
A character reference sheet is an image showing the same character from several angles and
with different expressions. It gives later generations a visual target. A name or a short
description alone leaves many details undecided, so each image can interpret the character
differently.
Ask ChatGPT for a brief covering three personality words, one funny habit or short catchphrase,
face and body details, and a simple outfit with clearly specified colours. Use plain clothes
without logos, patterns or writing. Simple, distinctive features are easier to compare and reuse
than a crowded design.
Use the course characters as an example
Golu is a six-year-old Indian boy presented as a little explorer. His established outfit is a yellow
T-shirt, blue shorts and red sandals. Chiku is his pet squirrel and best friend, described as a tiny
troublemaker. Their contrasting personalities give the stories an easy starting point: curiosity
from Golu and playful behaviour from Chiku.
For your own characters, approve the exact colour choices and record them in the brief. You can
use hexadecimal colour values to make these choices more specific. Keep the chosen values
unchanged in later prompts and compare each new result with the approved sheet.
Specify the reference-sheet layout
- Generate a separate sheet for each character, using a plain light-grey background and a wide
16:9 layout.
- Top row: four full-body views - front, three-quarter, side profile and back. Clothing, body
proportions and identifying features must match across the row.
- Bottom row: four face close-ups - happy, surprised, sad and angry. Change the expression
while keeping the character identity recognisable.
- Request no text, no labels and no background scenery. These sheets are visual references, not
illustrated title cards.
Reuse the exact Master Style line
Copy this line at the start of image and video prompts
Style: Soft, colourful, high-quality 3D animated kids' cartoon, rounded character shapes,
smooth clay-like textures, warm gentle lighting, expressive oversized eyes, friendly Indian
children's animation aesthetic, clean polished rendering, consistent character proportions.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 4; All Prompts pp. 1-2; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 02  /  GENERATE, TEST AND APPROVE
Designing Characters and Reference Sheets
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Build and inspect both sheets
1. Request separate prompts. Give ChatGPT the approved character briefs and ask for one
ready-to-use sheet prompt per character. Require the exact same Master Style line and the
specified eight-part layout in both prompts.
2. Generate the images. Use the image workflow demonstrated in Google Flow with Nano
Banana Pro, or the corresponding available option. Check the chosen aspect ratio and keep the
character brief beside you while reviewing the result.
3. Compare every view. Look for changes in hairstyle, face shape, clothing colour, shoes,
body size or distinguishing features. Inspect the side and back views as carefully as the front
view. Regenerate a flawed sheet before it becomes a reference.
4. Save one approved version. Name each final sheet clearly and retain the prompt and
design brief. Avoid mixing competing designs later.
Test the two characters together
Upload both approved sheets as reference images and request a simple shared scene. For
example, show Golu in a neighbourhood park with Chiku sitting on his shoulder. The prompt
should identify which reference belongs to each character and explicitly preserve both
appearances. Begin with the same Master Style line, use 16:9 and request no text.
The purpose is to test whether both designs remain recognisable when placed together.
Compare face shapes, outfits, relative size and overall rendering style. For this controlled test,
avoid multiple actions, unusual camera angles or elaborate scenery.
Diagnose common inconsistencies
A vague request such as "a cute Indian boy called Golu" can produce a different face, a different
animation style or unwanted lettering on the shirt. Correct this by supplying the approved sheet,
restoring the Master Style line and describing the specific mismatch.
Preserve successful details when retrying. Instructions such as "keep the same face, hairstyle,
outfit and proportions as the reference" help state the target, but they still require visual review.
Do not accept a sheet merely because one of its eight views looks correct.
Practice task and completion check
Create and approve one sheet for each of your two characters, then generate a simple image
containing both. Submit the sheets, the test image and the saved Master Style line. Confirm that
all views agree, expressions remain recognisable, clothing has no unwanted writing and the
shared image preserves both identities.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 4; All Prompts pp. 1-2; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: DESIGN THE WORLD
videos.description: Build three reusable settings for your cartoon series: a home, a neighbourhood street and a classroom. Learn to generate clean location references, maintain a shared visual style and combine characters with an approved setting. You will practise checking room layouts, character scale and background details so future scenes feel connected.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 03  /  DESIGN THE WORLD
Creating Consistent Locations and Sets
Build a small visual world that can support many episodes.
What a location reference does
A location set is an approved image of a place where your story can happen. It records the
layout, colours, furniture and atmosphere that should remain recognisable when the setting
returns. Treat it like a reusable set: the action may change, but the underlying environment
should still belong to the same world.
A written instruction such as "Golu's house in India" does not establish a particular room or
cartoon style. The course demonstrates that a vague request can produce a realistic photograph
instead. A clear prompt, the established Master Style line and an approved visual reference
make the intended result more explicit.
Start with the three course locations
Keeping a small set of locations helps you focus on storytelling and consistency. It also makes
the references easier to organise and reuse. You can tell several different stories in one
approved room; a new episode does not automatically require a new background.
- Home: a small, cosy Indian living room. It provides a familiar setting for everyday problems,
conversations and objects such as the plate of laddoos in the first episode.
- Neighbourhood: a narrow, colourful Indian street. It becomes a reusable outdoor setting for
playful actions and the rhyme project.
- School: a cheerful classroom in a small Indian school. It provides a third setting for future
stories without redesigning the entire series.
Write a clear location prompt
Ask ChatGPT for three separate image prompts, one for each location. Begin every prompt with
the exact Master Style line used for the character sheets. Specify a simple, clear layout in a wide
16:9 view, with no people, characters or animals.
Describe only the details needed to establish the space. Keep room features and major objects
easy to recognise. Request no text and no signs containing words. Leave enough uncluttered
space for characters to be added later rather than filling every part of the image with
decoration.
Why the first version should be empty
Separate the set from the performance
An empty reference lets you reuse the environment with different characters and actions. If a
character is already built into the location image, that pose or appearance can become
unwanted information in a later scene.
Sources: Course Notes p. 2; All Prompts pp. 2-3; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2, 5-7.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 03  /  TEST THE SET WITH YOUR CHARACTERS
Creating Consistent Locations and Sets
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Generate and approve the empty locations
1. Create one image per location. Use the image workflow demonstrated in Google Flow.
Keep the same style description and aspect ratio across all three sets so they feel like parts of
one series.
2. Check the layout. Inspect doors, windows, furniture, walkable space and the main colours.
Reject a location that contains unintended characters, unreadable writing or a completely
different rendering style.
3. Save the accepted references. Name each location clearly and save its prompt. Choose an
approved version before creating story scenes; repeated redesigns make continuity harder to
assess.
Combine the characters and the environment
Upload three references: Golu's sheet, Chiku's sheet and the approved living-room image. Ask
for a simple composition, such as Golu sitting on the sofa reading a picture book while Chiku
peeks from behind a cushion. Focus this test on appearance and placement.
Tell the model which reference defines each character and which one defines the room. Request
the same character designs, the same room layout and a believable size relationship between
Golu, Chiku and the furniture. Keep the Master Style line, 16:9 format and no-text instruction.
Check continuity and correct the cause
Compare the test image with all three references. Has the sofa moved to another wall? Have the
windows changed? Does Chiku suddenly appear almost as large as Golu? Is the room still
rendered in the same soft 3D style? Attractive images can still fail continuity checks.
If the room changes, confirm that the location image was included and explicitly preserve its
layout and major objects. If the style becomes photographic, restore the exact Master Style line.
If character size changes, describe the intended relationship to the other character and nearby
furniture. Change the relevant instruction, then review the new result against the same
approved references.
Practice task and completion check
Create three empty location references for your series and one test image combining both
characters with a location. Keep these references ready for the story-planning lesson.
- Each location is empty, clearly arranged and visually consistent with the characters.
- The test image preserves the approved room features and character identities.
- Character scale, furniture size and available action space make sense together.
Sources: Course Notes p. 2; All Prompts pp. 2-3; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2, 5-7.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: STORY AND SCENE PLANNING
videos.description: Learn to develop a short cartoon story with a clear beginning, an engaging problem and a meaningful ending. Using Golu and Chiku’s first episode, you will break the story into manageable scenes, plan simple actions and dialogue, and review the content for young audiences before starting animation.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 04  /  STORY AND SCENE PLANNING
Write Your First Cartoon Story
Turn a simple idea into a clear, child-friendly scene plan.
What this lesson helps you do
A useful animation script describes something the viewer can see and understand. In this lesson,
you develop one small problem, a clear discovery, and a simple moral. The course example is
Chiku and the Missing Laddoo: a sweet disappears, Golu suspects Chiku, and the explanation
shows why we should check before blaming someone.
The intended audience is children aged 3-8. Use familiar words, warm reactions, and a
straightforward sequence. The goal is to finish a story that can be produced with your existing
characters and locations.
Build a focused story brief
1. Keep the series context available. Continue in the working ChatGPT conversation, or
provide your saved character descriptions, catchphrases, and approved locations again. A
request such as 'write a children's story' gives too little direction and may introduce unrelated
characters.
2. Define the episode in one sentence. State the missing-laddoo problem, the
misunderstanding, and the moral: 'Do not blame someone before checking the facts.' Ask for a
short, funny, gentle story of about one minute, using only your established cast and settings.
3. Choose the simplest setting. The demonstration keeps this episode in the living room.
Remaining in one familiar place reduces background changes and makes the cause and effect
easier to follow. Include the characters' established catchphrases naturally without adding extra
scenes merely to fit them in.
Convert the story into a production-ready scene table
Ask for these columns: scene number, location, characters, one visible action, dialogue with the
speaker's name, and camera framing. Choose wide shots to show the setting, medium shots for
an action, or close-ups for a reaction or important prop.
The course uses eight scenes of eight seconds each, giving 64 seconds before editing or title
cards. Keep each spoken line around ten simple words or fewer, then read it aloud to check the
timing. One scene should communicate one main action; separate a complicated sequence into
simpler beats.
Common mistakes and corrections
A generic story usually needs a clearer brief, not more descriptive adjectives. Reintroduce the
cast, setting, age range, and moral. If a scene requires several actions, simplify it before making
any images. If dialogue feels rushed, shorten the line instead of asking the voice to speak faster.
Keep the moral connected to the discovery. A final message about checking facts works because
Golu first misunderstood the situation and then corrected his assumption.
Sources: Course Notes p. 2; All Prompts p. 3; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 3, 5, 7.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 04  /  REVIEW AND PRACTICE
Write Your First Cartoon Story
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
An illustrative eight-scene outline
Illustrative English outline: all eight scenes take place in the approved living room. Add
character presence, dialogue and camera framing when creating your own complete scene
table.
SceneOne main action
1Golu notices two laddoos on a plate.
2One laddoo accidentally rolls off while Golu looks away.
3Golu notices that one laddoo is missing.
4Golu gently asks Chiku about the missing sweet.
5Chiku points towards the fallen laddoo.
6Golu looks down and discovers what happened.
7Golu apologises to Chiku for the misunderstanding.
8The narrator shares the moral over a calm final pose.
Run a child-suitability check
- Check the emotional tone: Golu should ask kindly, without shouting, threatening, or humiliating
Chiku. The misunderstanding should feel small and reassuring.
- Check the physical action: the laddoo falls accidentally. Avoid climbing, risky chasing, or
sending Chiku behind furniture. Nobody eats food that has fallen on the floor.
- Check the explanation: show enough evidence for a young viewer to understand where the
laddoo went. The ending must resolve the same problem introduced at the beginning.
- Check the language: remove difficult words and long speeches. Ask ChatGPT to revise the
complete scene table after the review, so you have one final version to animate.
Your assignment
Write your own one-sentence episode idea and create an eight-row scene table. Read the
dialogue aloud, check that each row contains one main action, and complete the child-suitability
review. Save the approved table with your character and location references. You are ready for
Lesson 05 when someone can understand the story simply by reading its scenes in order.
Sources: Course Notes p. 2; All Prompts p. 3; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 3, 5, 7.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: PREPARE THE START FRAME
videos.description: Develop your first complete cartoon episode with character voices and narration. Learn to build a voice bible, organise production instructions for each scene, time short dialogue and connect consecutive clips using suitable final frames. The lesson also explains how to review voice consistency, visual continuity and the overall flow of your finished story.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 05  /  PREPARE THE START FRAME
Animate Your First Two Scenes
Build a clean start frame and turn one simple action into video.
Why the first image matters
A start frame is the image at the beginning of a video scene. It establishes the character's
appearance, pose, props, composition, and location before movement begins. If Golu has the
wrong clothes or the room has changed in this image, the video starts with those mistakes
already present.
This lesson produces the first two scenes without spoken dialogue. Working on movement first
makes it easier to notice visual problems. Voices and detailed speech timing are added in
Lesson 06 after you understand the image-to-video process.
Prepare the references and scene instructions
1. Read the approved scene row. Identify the location, visible characters, important props,
camera framing, and the single action. Decide what the viewer should see at the beginning,
before that action occurs. Do not try to show the entire scene inside one still image.
2. Collect the correct visual references. For a scene showing Golu at home, use Golu's
approved character sheet and the living-room image. Add Chiku's sheet if Chiku is visible. Select
the actual saved references rather than relying only on character names.
3. Request a start-frame image prompt. Ask ChatGPT for a prompt using your exact Master
Style line, the chosen references, and a description of the opening moment. State that the
character and room must match the references. Keep the composition 16:9 and request no text.
Generate and approve the image
In the course demonstration, image creation uses Google Flow's image workflow with Nano
Banana Pro. Upload the references, paste the prepared prompt, and generate the scene image.
Menu labels and available models may differ from the recording; use the corresponding
image-generation option available to you.
Inspect the result before animating it. Compare the face, clothes, body proportions, furniture,
lighting, and prop count against the references. The opening example places Golu in the living
room looking at a plate with two laddoos. Regenerate an incorrect frame before continuing.
A clear start-frame request
Approve this still image first. The video prompt will describe the single movement that follows,
rather than asking the image prompt to show several moments at once.
Illustrative English prompt - after the Master Style line
Using the uploaded Golu character sheet and living-room reference, show Golu looking at a
plate containing exactly two laddoos. Match his face, clothes and proportions and preserve
the room layout. Use a medium 16:9 composition, with no extra characters, no text and no
watermarks.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 3-4; All Prompts pp. 3-4; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5, 7-8.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 05  /  GENERATE, REVIEW, REPEAT
Animate Your First Two Scenes
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Turn the approved image into a video
1. Write the motion instruction. Give ChatGPT the approved start frame and the scene's
action. Request one simple movement, a static camera or another uncomplicated camera
instruction, and soft ambient sound. Include the Master Style line and explicitly say that there is
no dialogue yet.
2. Use the start-frame workflow. The course uses Flow's Video > Frames workflow: select
the approved image as the start frame and add the motion prompt. Demonstration settings are
16:9, eight seconds, and 720p where those options are available. These are course settings, not
a promise that every model or account presents identical choices.
3. Understand the mode distinction. Frames begins from a specified image. Ingredients
uses reference images without defining that same fixed opening frame. For this lesson, choose
the workflow that starts from your approved scene image so the planned composition guides the
animation.
Keep the motion instruction narrow
This is a teaching example, not the original scene transcript. Avoid combining walking, picking
up an object, speaking, and turning the camera in the same short clip.
Illustrative English instruction
After your Master Style line: 'Over eight seconds, Golu gently raises his eyebrows in curiosity
while looking at the plate. Keep his face, outfit, proportions, props, and room consistent with
the start frame. ONE ACTION ONLY. Static medium shot. No dialogue, no text, and no
additional characters. Soft room ambience only.'
Review the full clip before accepting it
Watch from beginning to end. Check whether the intended action is understandable, the
character stays recognisable, the room remains stable, and no extra text, people, or objects
appear. Compare the final moment with the opening rather than judging only the first frame.
If movement fails but the start frame is good, simplify the action prompt and regenerate from
that same image. If the start frame is wrong, correct it first. Reference instructions improve
control but do not guarantee a perfect result, so review every accepted clip.
Your assignment
Produce Scenes 1 and 2 using this complete sequence: scene row, references, approved start
frame, motion prompt, video, and review. Save each frame and accepted clip with a clear scene
number. Play both clips together to check that character appearance, prop positions, and the
story's order remain understandable before adding voices.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 3-4; All Prompts pp. 3-4; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5, 7-8.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

Step 2: Scene video prompt (Frames mode)

videos.title: PLAN THE FULL PRODUCTION
videos.description: Develop your first complete cartoon episode with character voices and narration. Learn to build a voice bible, organise production instructions for each scene, time short dialogue and connect consecutive clips using suitable final frames. The lesson also explains how to review voice consistency, visual continuity and the overall flow of your finished story.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 06  /  PLAN THE FULL PRODUCTION
Produce the Complete Episode with Voices
Coordinate voice direction, scene timing, and visual continuity.
From individual scenes to a complete episode
A complete episode needs more than eight attractive clips: the characters, setting, voices, and
story must connect. Begin with the final scene table, approved character sheets, location
images, Master Style line, and the scene-generation method practised in Lesson 05.
The course example uses eight clips of eight seconds each. Their untrimmed total is 64 seconds;
adding a title card or changing the edit can alter the final running time. Plan all scenes together
before generating them so missing dialogue or continuity problems are easier to catch.
Create a reusable voice bible
A voice bible is a saved description of how each speaker should sound. Ask ChatGPT for one
fixed English direction for Golu, Chiku, and the narrator, covering tone, pitch, speaking speed,
energy, and cartoon character. Reuse the approved wording whenever that speaker appears.
Choose one distinct direction for each speaker and save the approved wording. These
descriptions guide generation; they do not guarantee an identical voice in every clip.
Illustrative English voice directions
Golu: A curious, cheerful child-character voice, medium-high pitch, clear words, a relaxed
pace and playful energy. Chiku: A light, lively cartoon voice, higher pitch, short clear phrases
and friendly mischief. Narrator: A warm, gentle storytelling voice with a relaxed pace, clear
pronunciation and reassuring energy.
Build one production sheet for all eight scenes
- Start-frame instructions: provide either an image prompt with the required references or a
clear instruction to reuse a suitable last frame from the previous scene.
- Video instructions: include the exact Master Style line, one action, simple camera direction, the
dialogue, the correct voice description, and a timing block.
- Speaker control: identify who speaks and keep other characters silent during that line. Place
each scene's image and video prompts separately to avoid mixing instructions.
- Closing message: reserve the final scene for the narrator's simple moral, with enough time for
the line to finish clearly.
Check the sheet before generation
Read the scenes in order. Verify that each dialogue line belongs to the right speaker and that
the next scene follows logically from the previous action. If the script has changed, update the
approved table first so the story plan and production prompts do not contradict each other.
Sources: Course Notes p. 3; All Prompts p. 4; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5, 8.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 06  /  CONTINUITY, AUDIO, AND REVIEW
Produce the Complete Episode with Voices
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Reuse a last frame when the scene truly continues
When the next scene continues the same moment and setting, save a clean final frame from the
accepted video and use it as the next start frame. This carries visible positions, props, and
composition into the following shot and can reduce abrupt visual jumps.
Inspect that frame first: do not pass a distorted face, awkward pose, or misplaced object into
another generation. A new location or deliberately different shot may need a newly composed
start frame using the original reference images. Reusing a frame improves visual continuity but
does not automatically preserve movement or voice identity.
Give dialogue time to breathe
Use a timing block to separate the opening pose, speech, and final reaction. An illustrative
eight-second pattern is 0-1 seconds to settle, 1-5 seconds for a short line, and 5-8 seconds for a
gentle reaction. Adapt this timing to the actual scene rather than forcing every line into the
same pattern.
Keep dialogue short and specify 'only Golu speaks' or the appropriate speaker. For an on-camera
line, request mouth movement only during audible speech. The course limits on-camera
speaking to one or two scenes and uses more off-camera delivery elsewhere, reducing the
amount of lip-sync that needs careful review.
Generate in order and compare the results
Accept a scene only after checking its action, visual references, spoken words, and speaker.
Listen to adjacent clips together: changes in pitch, delivery, loudness, or background sound can
be more obvious at a cut than in isolation.
If the voice changes, reapply the exact voice-bible wording and regenerate the affected clip.
Where greater consistency is needed, use a consistent recorded or prepared voice track in
CapCut and align it with the picture. Keep speech understandable and leave the detailed music
mix for the editing lesson.
Your assignment and acceptance check
Produce all eight scenes with the approved dialogue and narration, then assemble a rough
sequence. Confirm that the story is clear, each speaker is identifiable, character and room
changes have been corrected, and no line is cut off. Finish with the moral: 'Do not blame
someone before checking the facts.' Save the voice bible, production sheet, frames, and
accepted clips for the final edit.
Sources: Course Notes p. 3; All Prompts p. 4; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5, 8.

videos.title: PLAN AND PRODUCE THE RHYME
videos.description: Create an original rhyme video using the characters, locations and voice references developed earlier. Learn to plan short musical clips, connect scenes through their final frames and manage audio consistency. The lesson also provides practical methods for correcting character changes, unwanted objects, rushed actions, lip-sync issues and other common generation problems.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 07  /  PLAN AND PRODUCE THE RHYME
Original Rhyme Videos and
Troubleshooting
Turn a short rhyme into a coherent video and diagnose common generation problems.
The purpose of this lesson
A rhyme video reuses the same production foundations as a story episode: approved character
sheets, a fixed Master Style line, a location reference and a clear action plan. The difference is
that the words, movement and rhythm must work together. In the course example, Chiku's Leap
takes place in the neighbourhood street. Golu sings while Chiku performs the actions.
The target is four verses with two short lines per verse. Each verse becomes one eight-second
clip, giving 32 seconds before editing. Keep the language familiar to children aged 3-8 and make
each action easy to understand visually. These English notes explain the process; the course
demonstration uses Hindi lyrics.
Write lyrics that fit the animation
1. Choose one simple theme. Use a small, friendly activity that suits the existing characters
and location. Keep the lyrics original instead of copying a familiar nursery rhyme.
2. Request a timed draft. Ask ChatGPT for four two-line verses with a steady, bouncy rhythm.
Read or sing each verse aloud within eight seconds. Shorten difficult words and crowded lines
before generating video.
3. Assign one visible action. Give each clip one movement matching its verse, such as a
small hop. Avoid combining jumping, running, turning and waving in the same eight seconds.
Build the four-clip production sheet
For every clip, record the verse, singer, action, start frame, references, camera and timing.
Begin each prompt with the exact Master Style line. Include the singer's unchanged voice-bible
description and specify who sings. Request no background music so the soundtrack can be
controlled during editing.
Create Clip 1's start frame from the character sheets and street reference. When the action
continues directly, use the previous approved clip's last frame for Clips 2-4. Check that this
frame is clean and suitable for the next action; otherwise create a fresh, matching start frame.
Check audio as carefully as the picture
Repeated voice instructions can help, but separate generations may still change the melody,
pitch or pronunciation. Listen to all four clips in sequence. A background track will not
automatically fix mismatched singing. If needed, use one consistent vocal recording in CapCut
and align the pictures to it.
Sources: Course Notes p. 3; All Prompts pp. 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 3, 5, 8-9.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 07  /  DIAGNOSE, CORRECT AND REVIEW
Original Rhyme Videos and Troubleshooting
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
A practical troubleshooting reference
These prompt additions clarify the intended result; they cannot guarantee a perfect generation.
First inspect the source references and start frame. Keep successful inputs unchanged, correct
one problem at a time and compare the new clip with the approved design.
Problem / likely causePrompt adjustment or practical fix
Face or outfit changes: design is
being reinterpreted.
STRICT CHARACTER LOCK: match the reference face, hair, colours,
clothing and proportions; no redesign.
Extra or merged fingers: small
hands or complex gestures.
HAND ANATOMY LOCK: preserve the approved hand or paw
anatomy; use simple gestures; no extra or fused digits.
Voice changes: each clip is a
separate generation.
Repeat the exact voice-bible line. If variation persists, use
consistent recorded audio in CapCut.
Lip-sync drifts: speech is crowded or
timing is unclear.
Shorten the line. Mouth movement only while the named character
speaks; keep other mouths closed.
Size or room changes: scale and
layout lack references.
SCALE AND ENVIRONMENT LOCK: retain the location layout, prop
positions and relative character sizes.
Random text appears: the model
adds surface details.
NO TEXT RULE: no letters, numbers, signs, captions, logos or
watermarks in this scene.
Extra characters appear: the
background is being populated.
CHARACTER COUNT LOCK: only Golu and Chiku appear; no
additional people or animals.
Action feels rushed: too many
events share one clip.
ONE ACTION ONLY: specify one movement, a timing block and a
static or simple camera.
Correct the cause before regenerating
A wrong face in the start frame is already a continuity problem; fix that image first. For hand
problems, compare against the character sheet. A human hand may need five fingers when that
matches the approved design, but a squirrel's paws must follow its own reference. Do not apply
one anatomy instruction to every character.
If a clip contains several faults, simplify the shot before adding more instructions. Fewer
gestures, shorter lyrics and a calmer camera give the model a clearer task. Regenerate the
affected clip and review its joins with the clips immediately before and after it.
Practice task and completion check
Produce one original four-clip rhyme and save the final lyrics, production sheet and approved
videos. Confirm that the same characters and location remain recognisable, words are clear,
actions match the lyrics and transitions feel continuous. Record one problem, the change you
made and whether it improved the result. Keep this troubleshooting record for future episodes.
Sources: Course Notes p. 3; All Prompts pp. 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 3, 5, 8-9.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

Chhalaang]", set in [location].

lines that rhyme, easy to sing in 8 seconds, with a bouncy nursery-rhyme rhythm. Both

2) A Google Flow video prompt with our Master Style line, ONE simple action that matches

Each prompt in its own code box.

Make me a quick troubleshooting table for Google Flow cartoon videos with 3 columns:
Problem | Why it happens | Exact line to add or change in the prompt.
Cover: character's face or outfit changes, extra or merged fingers, voice changes between

videos.title: EDIT AND PACKAGE THE EPISODE
videos.description: Bring your completed scenes together in CapCut and prepare the episode for publication. Learn to balance dialogue and music, create a clear thumbnail, write accurate titles and descriptions, and review audience settings. Complete your first episode, perform a final quality check and develop a practical plan for future stories.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 08  /  EDIT AND PACKAGE THE EPISODE
Editing, Thumbnails and Publishing Your
Series
Assemble the final episode, prepare its presentation and build a repeatable release plan.
From generated clips to a complete story
The final lesson turns separate assets into an episode that a viewer can follow comfortably.
Gather the eight approved scene videos, the final scene table, any replacement voice recordings
and the character references. Use the table to check the sequence. Eight eight-second clips
provide 64 seconds of source footage; the final duration can change when you trim shots or add
a title card.
The course example is Chiku and the Missing Laddoo. Its ending should clearly explain the
misunderstanding and the lesson: check the facts before blaming someone. Editing should
support that story rather than distract from it.
Assemble and review in CapCut
1. Arrange the scenes. Import the clips and place them in story order. Watch each cut for
changes in pose, props, character scale and room layout. Trim only where the action and
dialogue still make sense.
2. Add a simple opening. Create a short title card such as Golu & Chiku - Episode 1. Keep it
readable and brief. If captions are added, check their spelling and timing and avoid covering
important actions.
3. Balance the sound. Keep voices easy to hear and lower the music underneath them. Use
suitable music that you are permitted to use. Remove unwanted duplicate audio when replacing
a generated voice.
4. Export and watch the file. Follow the course's 1080p export workflow and preserve the
16:9 frame. Review the exported video from beginning to end. Exporting a 720p source at
1080p changes output size but does not recreate missing detail.
Design a thumbnail with a clear focal point
Provide both character sheets and one episode frame as references. Keep the image bright and
simple: Golu's surprised expression, Chiku peeking and the laddoo clearly visible. Use the
approved visual style and a 16:9 composition.
Request only the intended short headline, such as Where Is the Laddoo? This is a deliberate
exception to the no-text rule used for scene generation. Check every letter; if generated spelling
is wrong, create the artwork without text and add the headline manually. Preview the thumbnail
at a small size before approving it.
Sources: Course Notes p. 4; All Prompts p. 5; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 4-5, 9-10.
