SKILLOMATEAI CARTOON SERIES  |  GOLU & CHIKU
LESSON 08  /  PUBLISH AND PLAN THE NEXT EPISODES
Editing, Thumbnails and Publishing Your Series
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Write accurate publishing information
Ask ChatGPT for an episode title, a short description and ten relevant tags based on the finished
story. Include the series or episode name where useful and describe what the viewer will
actually see. For this example, mention the missing laddoo, Golu and Chiku, and the lesson
about checking before blaming. Avoid promises about learning results, popularity or other
benefits the episode does not demonstrate.
Read the title and description alongside the thumbnail. They should introduce the same story
and use the same names. Tags should relate to the actual episode; they do not replace clear
content or accurate presentation.
Choose audience and visibility settings carefully
The demonstration series is specifically created for children aged 3-8. Set the audience
accordingly using YouTube's Made for Kids designation and review the current guidance during
upload. This setting affects available features, including comments and personalised
advertising.
Use Unlisted for the initial review, then change the video to Public when the checks are
complete. An unlisted video can be viewed and shared by anyone with its link; it is not a private
approval space. Watch the uploaded version, including its beginning, scene transitions, audio,
ending and thumbnail, before making it public.
Make a sustainable series plan
Plan the next ten episodes using the same two characters and three established locations. For
each episode, write a title, a one-sentence story and one simple moral. Reusing approved assets
reduces repeated design decisions while allowing new situations and lessons.
The course suggests one episode per week and a two-episode buffer before starting regular
publication. Treat this as a practical planning target: allow time for writing, generation,
corrections and export. Reduce the schedule if the quality checks cannot be completed
comfortably. Keep finished episodes and reusable assets organised by episode and scene.
Final project: evidence of completion
Submit or save the completed episode with its thumbnail, title, description and ten-episode plan.
Keep the character sheets, location references, voice bible and production sheet so the next
episode starts from an established foundation.
- Story: a clear beginning, misunderstanding, resolution and simple moral.
- Picture: consistent characters and locations, readable actions and clean scene joins.
- Sound: intelligible dialogue, suitable pacing and music below the voices.
- Presentation: a checked export, accurate thumbnail and metadata, and appropriate upload
settings.
Sources: Course Notes p. 4; All Prompts p. 5; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 4-5, 9-10.

courses.title: Viral Hook Formula
courses.description:
Learn how to create clear, compelling openings for Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. Viral Hook Formula introduces eight practical approaches: curiosity gaps, pattern interrupts, bold statements, questions, stories, visuals, numbered lists and relatable POV scenes.

Across ten lessons, you will learn to write stronger first lines, plan effective opening visuals and connect every hook to a meaningful payoff. Practical examples and assignments help you choose the right approach for your audience, communicate your topic quickly and deliver the value your opening promises. You will also explore how to combine hook styles, use ChatGPT to develop relevant options and compare different openings to improve your content.

Designed for creators, small business owners and students, the course concludes with a practical project: creating eight original reels, one for each hook type, using a repeatable process for planning, reviewing and refining your ideas.

videos.title: HOOK FOUNDATIONS
videos.description: Understand what a hook does and how your first line, opening visual and promised payoff work together. Explore the eight hook types covered in the course, learn to recognise weak or misleading openings, and review your recent reels. You will begin building concise, relevant introductions that match the content you actually deliver.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 01  /  HOOK FOUNDATIONS
The First Three Seconds: Understanding
Hooks
Give viewers a clear reason to pay attention from the opening moment.
What a hook actually does
A hook is the opening line and visual that introduce a reason to keep watching a reel or short
video. It may raise a question, show an interesting result, introduce a problem or begin an
unexpected action. The viewer should quickly understand what makes this particular video
relevant, useful or entertaining.
The course focuses on the first three seconds as a practical creative target. This is not a fixed
platform rule or a guarantee that a video will be recommended. The purpose is to remove a slow
opening and communicate the idea promptly, while keeping speech natural and understandable.
Connect attention with a useful promise
A hook can help someone notice your content, but attention alone is not the finished job. The rest
of the video must answer the question or deliver the result introduced at the start. This delivery is
the payoff. A clear promise also helps you decide which information belongs in the reel.
In the introductory demonstration, the presenter asks the viewer to stop scrolling and then
explains the technique she has just used. Treat that as an example to analyse, not a phrase to
repeat in every video. Your own opening should give a reason connected to your audience and
topic.
Know the eight approaches you will practise
Later lessons combine these approaches, use ChatGPT to draft alternatives and compare two
openings for the same topic. There is no single format that fits every audience or video.
- Curiosity gap opens a specific question; pattern interrupt introduces a relevant unexpected
action, sound or visual.
- Bold statement challenges familiar advice with a reason; question directly addresses an
audience problem.
- Story begins at an interesting moment; visual uses the opening image itself to communicate
interest.
- List promises a clear number of points; POV recreates a specific situation the audience
recognises.
Use the course's central rule
A hook is a promise
Pair a specific opening line with a relevant first image, then deliver what they promise. Strong
wording cannot compensate for a missing answer, an unrelated video or a claim the content
cannot support.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 01  /  BUILD AND REVIEW YOUR OPENING
The First Three Seconds: Understanding Hooks
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Two illustrative English examples
These examples demonstrate the structure rather than guaranteeing performance. Notice how
each includes something to say, something to show and a result that the video can actually
provide.
- Product demonstration: "Here is the print this stamp makes." Opening visual: hold the stamp
above a clean sheet of paper, ready to press. Payoff: show the stamping action and a clear
close-up of the actual print. The opening and result refer to the same product.
- Study content: "Turn this paragraph into three revision questions." Opening visual: show one
short paragraph with the number three on screen. Payoff: demonstrate three questions drawn
from that paragraph. Keep all three questions visible long enough to read.
Write the opening before building the full reel
1. Choose the viewer and topic. Name the audience and one specific idea. A narrow topic
makes the opening easier to understand than a broad promise to explain everything.
2. Define the payoff. Write one sentence describing what the viewer will receive. Use this to
check that your proposed hook is accurate before filming.
3. Draft the line and first visual. Keep the spoken opening short and place the relevant
subject on screen immediately. Add a readable text overlay carrying the main idea.
4. Rehearse and review. Read the line naturally, then watch the opening with sound muted.
The image and text should still make the topic clear.
Correct common opening problems
If the video begins with a blank screen, long greeting or logo animation, move the useful content
earlier. If the line feels vague, name the exact problem or result. If it takes too long to say,
remove extra words rather than rushing your voice.
Do not diagnose every low-performing reel as a hook failure. The topic, content, delivery and
audience fit also matter. Use the opening review to identify something concrete you can
improve, without promising views or virality.
Your assignment
Write down the first line and describe the first visual of your last five reels. For each, identify the
promise and where the video fulfils it. Rewrite one weak opening. Check its clarity, natural
delivery, readability without sound and connection to the actual payoff.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: CREATE A QUESTION WORTH ANSWERING
videos.description: Learn to create curiosity by introducing a specific question, missing detail or surprising part of a process. Develop openings that give viewers a reason to continue, then plan a clear and timely payoff. You will practise writing five curiosity hooks while avoiding vague secrets, exaggerated claims and unnecessary delays.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 02  /  CREATE A QUESTION WORTH ANSWERING
The Curiosity Gap Hook
Open a meaningful question and reward the viewer with a clear answer.
Understand the curiosity gap
A curiosity gap is the space between what the viewer already sees or understands and one
detail they want to discover. The hook establishes the topic but leaves a specific question open.
The reel then closes that gap by showing or explaining the answer.
This approach suits demonstrations, useful tips and behind-the-scenes content when the missing
detail genuinely matters. The viewer needs enough context to care. Saying only "you will not
believe this" with no visible subject creates uncertainty, but it does not explain why the answer
is worth watching.
Use a clear, honest formula
The course demonstrates phrases about an undisclosed secret. Keep the useful structure while
avoiding unsupported claims such as "nobody knows this" or "every creator hides this." Describe
the specific detail you can show instead of inventing exclusivity.
Curiosity formula
Start with a recognisable topic or result, identify one unanswered detail, and reveal it through
the video. Example structure: "One step changes this result." Show what the step is and how
it fits the process.
Plan the answer before recording
1. Choose a useful missing detail. Identify an ingredient, process step, design choice or
explanation that belongs to your topic. The answer should be more substantial than a generic
reminder to keep watching.
2. Write the opening promise. State the question or withheld detail in one short line. Avoid
adding a second mystery that the same video cannot resolve.
3. Choose the opening image. Show the result, object or situation the question refers to. The
visual should make the gap easier to understand without revealing everything at once.
4. Map the reveal. Decide when to show the answer and what evidence or demonstration
makes it clear. Then build the remaining script around that delivery.
Make the waiting worthwhile
The source lesson places its answer near the end, but that is one structure rather than a rule.
Reveal the useful detail as soon as the story or demonstration supports it. Give relevant
information along the way; repeated promises to reveal a secret create delay without value.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 02  /  EXAMPLES, CORRECTIONS AND PRACTICE
The Curiosity Gap Hook
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Three illustrative English examples
- Food preparation: "What gives this sandwich its crunch?" Opening visual: show the finished
sandwich being cut, with filling partly visible. Payoff: reveal and demonstrate the crisp
vegetable layer used in this sandwich. Avoid claiming it is a secret used by every restaurant.
- Product packaging: "There is one more detail inside this parcel." Opening visual: show an open
box containing the product, with a partly covered insert. Payoff: reveal the care-instruction
card and explain its purpose. Use this only when the detail is included.
- Content creation: "One choice comes before I film this reel." Opening visual: show a blank shot
list beside a written opening line. Payoff: explain the course practice of drafting the hook first,
then planning the reel to deliver its promise.
Recognise a weak or misleading gap
An opening can be intriguing but still disappoint if the answer does not match the question. A
promise about a specific technique should end with that technique, not an unrelated promotion.
Check the payoff in plain language: does it resolve exactly what you asked?
Avoid presenting an ordinary tip as a universal secret or a guaranteed solution. For example, a
broad claim that one mistake explains all poor results is harder to support than a demonstration
of one issue in a particular example. Make the claim no larger than the evidence in your reel.
Tighten the delivery
Read the hook aloud and remove phrases that repeat the same promise. Replace "stay until the
very end and I will finally tell you" with a shorter setup, then move into the relevant explanation.
If the answer fits near the beginning, reveal it there and use the remaining time to show how it
works.
Keep the hook visible in a short text overlay when useful. Do not hide all context just to preserve
suspense: a viewer should still recognise the topic and understand what question remains
unanswered.
Your assignment and review
Write five curiosity hooks for your own niche. Beside each, describe the opening visual, the
exact answer and the point in the reel where it appears. Choose one and rehearse a short
version. Confirm that the question is specific, the reveal is meaningful and no unnecessary delay
separates the viewer from the promised value.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: MAKE THE INTERRUPTION MEAN SOMETHING
videos.description: Explore how an unexpected action, sound or visual change can create an engaging opening. Learn to connect the interruption directly to your topic, pair it with a clear message and deliver the promised content. You will plan and rehearse an opening that feels purposeful, readable and practical to film.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 03  /  MAKE THE INTERRUPTION MEAN SOMETHING
The Pattern Interrupt Hook
Use a relevant surprise to introduce the subject of your reel.
What a pattern interrupt is
A pattern interrupt changes an expected opening. Instead of beginning with a greeting or a
static introduction, the reel starts with a noticeable action, sound, movement or change in
framing. The difference can help draw attention, especially when similar videos use similar
introductions.
The effect is a creative device, not a reliable way to control every viewer or guarantee
distribution. Its purpose is to make the subject noticeable and lead immediately into relevant
content. An interruption that has no connection to the topic may attract a glance without giving
anyone a reason to continue.
Understand the demonstration
In the course opening, the presenter tears a piece of paper and identifies it as an old content
plan before introducing a new one. The action acts as a simple visual metaphor: an existing
approach is being replaced. The accompanying line explains why the viewer has just seen it.
You can adapt that idea without using the same action. For example, turn over a rough draft to
reveal a revised plan. The useful element is the relationship between the physical change and
the lesson that follows, not the dramatic gesture by itself.
Build the hook with three linked parts
- Action: reveal, turn, lift, place or open something that already belongs to the topic.
- Sound: use a recognisable sound from the real activity, such as an egg cracking into a bowl.
- Framing: begin unusually close to a meaningful detail, then reveal the wider context.
Pattern interrupt formula
Unexpected but relevant opening action + a short line that explains its meaning + an
immediate transition into the promised content. The movement should introduce the idea
rather than become a separate performance.
Choose one clear interruption
Start with one deliberate change. Stacking a loud effect, sudden zoom, thrown object and
several captions can make the idea harder to read. Plan an ordinary, controlled action that fits
your filming space. Keep the subject in focus and leave enough space for the movement. One
clear action is easier to connect with the following shot than several simultaneous effects.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 03  /  PLAN, FILM AND REVIEW
The Pattern Interrupt Hook
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Three illustrative English examples
- Content planning: "This plan forgot the editing." Opening visual: turn over a crowded draft to
reveal three clear production slots. Payoff: explain how the revised plan separates writing,
filming and editing. Use the contrast to introduce the planning method.
- Cooking: "Start with this egg." Opening visual and sound: crack an egg into a bowl in a clear
close-up. Payoff: continue directly into the preparation shown in the reel. The sound comes
from the subject instead of an unrelated audio effect.
- Fashion: "Same scarf, a different finish." Opening visual: lift a scarf across the frame, then
lower it to reveal its starting position. Payoff: demonstrate one complete styling change. Keep
the movement controlled and ensure the garment is easy to see.
Create a simple filming plan
1. Name the content promise. Write what the viewer will learn or see. Choose an interruption
that represents this idea rather than adding an unrelated stunt.
2. Rehearse the opening movement. Decide where the object begins, what moves and what
the camera reveals. Keep the action understandable within the opening moment.
3. Connect it with one line. Say or display a short explanation of the action. If sound supplies
the surprise, also make the subject clear in the image or text.
4. Continue without a reset. Move directly into the demonstration or explanation. Avoid a
second introduction after the interruption, because it delays the promised content.
Correct the most common mistakes
If the action looks striking but the topic remains unclear, change the accompanying line or
choose an object that explains the subject better. If the sound is the only meaningful element,
add a clear image or text cue for viewers watching without audio.
If the opening feels crowded, remove extra effects and keep one movement. If viewers must
wait through a long greeting after the action, shorten that transition. The interruption and payoff
should belong to the same idea.
Your assignment and review
Plan one unexpected opening for your next reel. Write its action, line, first visual and payoff,
then record a short rehearsal. Review it with and without sound. Check that the surprise is
relevant, the subject is understandable and the video can continue naturally into the promised
content.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1-2, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-3, 5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: UNDERSTAND THE FORMULA
videos.description: Learn to create bold opening statements that challenge familiar advice without misleading your audience. This lesson explains how to choose a relevant belief, define the situation in which your alternative makes sense, and support the hook with a clear reason. You will practise turning strong opinions into useful, credible reel openings.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 04  /  UNDERSTAND THE FORMULA
Bold Statement (Contrarian) Hook
Challenge familiar advice with a clear, honest explanation.
What makes a statement contrarian?
A contrarian hook questions something your audience commonly hears or does. Instead of
repeating familiar advice, it introduces a different view and gives people a reason to ask, 'Why
would that be better here?' The useful part is the explanation that follows the statement.
The course opens this lesson with 'Stop posting daily,' followed by a preference for three good
reels over seven weak ones. Treat that comparison as an illustrative opinion about quality and
workload. It is not evidence that a particular posting frequency always produces better results.
Use a claim, reason, and demonstration
For example, 'Stop posting just to fill the calendar' can lead into advice for a solo creator who is
rushing unfinished ideas. Explain that, in this situation, reducing the workload creates room to
plan clearer scripts. Do not turn that observation into a claim that daily posting is wrong for
every creator.
Practical formula
Question a familiar habit + specify when your advice applies + give a clear reason + show a
useful alternative. The opening can be bold; the explanation must remain accurate.
Build the hook step by step
1. Choose advice your audience recognises. List common habits in your niche, such as
posting every day, highlighting entire pages, or opening product videos with lengthy packaging
shots. Pick one you can discuss specifically.
2. Find a genuine limitation. Ask when the habit becomes less useful. Describe the situation
and the practical tradeoff. If you cannot explain the limitation honestly, choose another idea
instead of forcing disagreement.
3. Plan the payoff before filming. Decide what the viewer will see: a clearer script, a more
selective set of notes, or the product working. Your opening should promise only what this
demonstration can deliver.
Keep the opening easy to understand
Say one short statement and move promptly into its reason. Use the first few seconds as a
creative guide, not a guarantee of distribution. A concise text overlay and a relevant first frame
help communicate the claim when sound is off.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 04  /  EXAMPLES AND PRACTICE
Bold Statement (Contrarian) Hook
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Three illustrative English examples
These are adaptable teaching examples. Use the claims only when the accompanying
explanation fits the content you actually make.
- Creator: 'Stop posting just to fill the calendar.' Opening visual: a crowded weekly plan beside
an unfinished script. Scope and reason: if daily deadlines leave your ideas unclear, reduce the
workload. Payoff: show one rushed outline being revised into a focused script and explain your
scheduling choice.
- Student: 'Stop highlighting every line.' Opening visual: a page where nearly every sentence is
coloured. Scope and reason: if everything is marked, the markings no longer identify what you
selected as important. Payoff: show a more selective page and explain why each marked
sentence supports the topic.
- Product: 'Stop opening this stamp demo with the box.' Opening visual: a finished stamp
impression beside its packaging. Scope and reason: in a demonstration about the printed
result, a long unboxing delays that result. Payoff: show the stamp being used and reveal the
finished design clearly.
Avoid empty controversy
A dramatic statement without a reason creates an argument rather than a useful lesson. Give
the reason immediately, then support it with a visible example. Avoid words such as 'always,'
'never,' or 'everyone' unless the claim genuinely supports that scope.
Do not invent results, statistics, or personal experience to make the claim sound authoritative.
Describe an opinion as an opinion and a demonstration as a demonstration. Disagree with the
advice respectfully; insulting people who follow it adds no practical value.
Check the promise against the finished reel
- Can the viewer identify the familiar advice you are questioning?
- Have you explained the situation in which your alternative applies?
- Does the footage actually show the reason or alternative you promised?
- Would the opening still be accurate if someone watched only that first line?
Your assignment
Choose one common piece of advice in your niche. Write a bold opening, a one-sentence
explanation, and a description of the first visual. Then outline the demonstration that will deliver
the payoff. Read the opening aloud, remove unnecessary words, and soften any claim that goes
beyond what your example can support.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: FIND THE RIGHT QUESTION
videos.description: Turn everyday audience problems into focused question hooks for Reels and Shorts. Learn to replace vague greetings with relevant questions, match the first visual to the problem, and provide a useful answer in the reel. Practical examples help you write openings that feel specific, natural and appropriate for your audience.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 05  /  FIND THE RIGHT QUESTION
Question Hook
Open with a specific question your audience already cares about.
Start with a recognisable problem
A question hook invites the viewer to think about a situation that matters to them. Its strength
comes from relevance: a creator, student, or customer should recognise the problem and
understand what the reel will help them explore. A question mark alone does not make an
opening useful.
The course contrasts specific questions with a general greeting such as 'Hello, how are you?' A
greeting can be friendly, but it gives little information about the topic. Begin with the audience's
problem and add any necessary introduction after the opening.
Use a specific situation and a clear question
Instead of 'Do you struggle with content?', ask 'Can viewers understand your opening with the
sound off?' The second version names something observable and gives the reel a clear task:
demonstrate how the opening communicates visually. Avoid putting several unrelated problems
into the same question.
Practical formula
Audience situation + precise problem or decision + a question the reel can answer. Pair the
words with a first frame that makes the situation visible.
Develop the hook in three steps
1. Write down the audience's actual situation. Use questions people have asked, problems
you have observed, or a clearly labelled teaching example. Be specific about the task: naming
assignment files, choosing a product size, or explaining a reel without audio.
2. Ask about something you can show. Choose one decision, difficulty, or point of confusion.
Use everyday language. A useful question should allow a concrete demonstration, comparison,
or explanation rather than a vague motivational answer.
3. Plan the answer and opening image together. Decide what appears in the first frame
and what the viewer will learn by the end. If the question concerns product size, show the
product and a relevant size reference rather than unrelated footage.
Avoid unsupported diagnoses
A weak opening can be worth reviewing, but do not claim to know why every viewer skips a reel.
Many factors may affect a result. Ask an observable question instead of declaring an unverified
cause. Keep the first line brief; the course's three-second target is a creative guideline, not an
algorithm rule.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 05  /  EXAMPLES AND PRACTICE
Question Hook
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Three illustrative English examples
Each example names one concern, makes it visible immediately, and delivers an answer within
the reel. Adapt the details to your own audience instead of copying the wording into an
unrelated topic.
- Creator: 'Does your opening make sense on mute?' Opening visual: play the first moment of a
sample reel without sound. Payoff: identify what is unclear, add a concise overlay or more
relevant opening shot, and compare the two versions. Keep the spoken question and text
overlay focused on the same issue.
- Student: 'Which file is your final assignment?' Opening visual: several similarly named files on a
demonstration screen. Payoff: show a simple naming example that includes the subject, task,
and version, then identify the submitted copy.
- Product: 'Will this stamp fit on your gift tag?' Opening visual: hold the actual stamp beside a
small tag. Payoff: show the measured print area and a test impression on that tag. Place the
real print measurements beside the impression so viewers can compare them with the tag.
Make the question easy to follow
Read the line aloud in a natural voice. Remove the greeting, long setup, and repeated words. Put
the essential question on screen in a readable overlay, and check that the image supports it
when sound is off.
The question should create a useful reason to continue. Begin answering promptly rather than
repeating 'wait until the end.' If the answer needs more explanation than a short reel allows,
narrow the question to one manageable part of the topic.
Common mistakes and corrections
- Too broad: replace 'Want better results?' with a question about one task or observable
difficulty.
- Too many questions: choose the one the reel answers most clearly and save the others for
separate videos.
- False assumption: avoid telling every viewer they have a problem. Ask whether the specific
situation applies to them.
- Missing payoff: show the answer, method, or comparison promised in the opening instead of
switching topics.
Your assignment
List three problems or decisions relevant to your audience. Turn each into one short question
hook. For every question, write the opening visual and the answer you can demonstrate. Select
the clearest option, record a rough opening, and review it both with sound and on mute before
planning the rest of the reel.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: CHOOSE THE TURNING POINT
videos.description: Learn to open a reel at the most interesting moment of a story. This lesson shows how to combine a clear time or place with an unexpected development, introduce background without slowing the opening, and deliver a meaningful resolution. You will practise shaping a real experience into a concise, engaging story hook.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 06  /  CHOOSE THE TURNING POINT
Story Hook: Start in the Middle
Begin at the turning point, then add only the background viewers need.
What does starting in the middle mean?
A story hook begins where something changes: a plan fails, a discovery appears, or a decision
becomes necessary. The viewer meets the situation at an interesting moment instead of hearing
a long history first. You can explain the essential background after giving them a reason to care
about the outcome.
In the course demonstration, a late-night message becomes the opening event for a story about
changing a content style. The useful structure is the specific moment followed by an unexpected
development. A story does not need a dramatic crisis; a small, relevant surprise can be enough.
Use time or place, then the twist
A time cue such as 'Before class' or a place cue such as 'At my kitchen counter' helps the viewer
enter the scene quickly. The twist should be specific: a file would not open, an ingredient was
missing, or a product test revealed a mistake. Avoid vague endings such as 'and everything
changed' unless you explain what changed.
Practical formula
A short time or place cue + the moment something changes + a clear reason to wonder what
happened next. Then add essential context, show the response, and resolve the story.
Build the opening from the event
1. Choose a genuine, useful moment. Pick an experience you can describe accurately and
connect to your audience. If you are making a fictional demonstration or reenactment, identify it
clearly rather than presenting an invented event as personal testimony.
2. Find the first visible change. Identify the exact action or discovery that makes the story
interesting. Start there. Remove the long introduction, routine preparation, and details that do
not affect the viewer's understanding.
3. Plan the resolution before filming. Write what you did next, what happened, and what
the viewer can take from it. The payoff must answer the question raised by the opening, even
when the outcome is modest or imperfect.
Keep the opening concise
Use the first few seconds to establish the moment, not the entire plot. Read the line aloud and
remove unnecessary words. The three-second target helps focus the writing; it does not
guarantee attention, reach, or a particular result.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3-4, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-2, 4-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 06  /  EXAMPLES AND PRACTICE
Story Hook: Start in the Middle
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Three illustrative English examples
These fictional scenarios illustrate the formula. Adapt them to a real experience, or label the
video as a demonstration. Do not present invented events as something that happened to you.
- Student: 'Before class, my presentation would not open.' Opening visual: a demonstration slide
file failing to load. Payoff: explain that the slides are needed immediately, open a saved PDF
backup and show the first slide. Finish by showing the backup folder the student will keep
ready next time.
- Cooking: 'At dinner, I noticed the bread was missing.' Opening visual: sandwich filling beside an
empty bread basket. Payoff: use an available wrap instead, add the filling, roll it and reveal the
finished meal. The story follows one practical adjustment from a missing ingredient to a
completed dish.
- Product: 'At my desk, the first stamp print was incomplete.' Opening visual: an imperfect
impression beside the stamp. Payoff: show that one corner missed the ink pad, ink the full
design and make a second impression. End with the complete print beside the first attempt so
the improvement is visible.
Add background only when it helps
After the opening event, give the minimum context needed to understand its importance. For
the presentation story, the viewer may need to know that class was starting soon. They do not
need the full history of the assignment before seeing what happened.
Continue with the character's response and the result. Match the visuals to those steps. A simple
sequence of problem, response, and outcome keeps the story understandable while preserving
the interest created by the opening.
Common mistakes and corrections
- Starting too early: cut routine background and begin at the moment the plan changes.
- Using an unclear twist: name the specific event instead of relying on 'something unbelievable
happened.'
- Adding unrelated details: keep only the context that explains the problem, response, or
outcome.
- Ending without resolution: show what happened next and address the exact question created
by the opening.
Your assignment
Choose one real moment from your life or work. Write a time-or-place opening that starts at its
turning point. Add one sentence of background, the action you took, and the outcome. Plan a
relevant first visual, read the sequence aloud, and remove any detail that delays the story
without helping the viewer understand it.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 3-4, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-2, 4-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: UNDERSTAND THE VISUAL PROMISE
videos.description: Learn to build visual openings using close-ups, movement and unusual camera angles. This lesson explains how to make the subject clear without relying on audio, connect the opening image to the reel’s promise and avoid delayed introductions. Practise planning first frames that lead naturally into useful, relevant content.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 07  /  UNDERSTAND THE VISUAL PROMISE
Visual Hooks: Make the First Frame Count
Create an opening image that introduces your topic clearly, even without sound.
What makes a hook visual?
A visual hook uses the opening image to introduce something worth noticing. It may show an
appealing detail, an action already in progress or a view the audience does not usually see. In
the lesson demonstration, the presenter brings a red apple towards the camera. The image
introduces the object before the spoken explanation adds meaning.
The goal is not simply to make an attractive frame. The viewer should be able to recognise a
subject and anticipate what the reel will show. A useful test is to watch the opening with the
sound off: can you identify the main object or situation, and does it connect to the content that
follows?
The formula and its three approaches
- Close-up: isolate a useful detail, such as steam rising from food or a product's texture. Keep
enough context for the detail to make sense.
- Movement: bring the subject into view or begin a meaningful action immediately. The
movement should reveal information instead of merely shaking the camera.
- Unusual angle: show a familiar subject from a fresh viewpoint, such as above a work surface.
Choose the angle because it makes the process clearer.
VISUAL HOOK FORMULA
Open with a relevant close-up, clear movement or unusual angle; reveal the subject quickly;
follow with the demonstration or explanation the image suggests.
Visual hook versus pattern interrupt
A visual hook communicates through what is seen. A pattern interrupt breaks an expected flow
with an unexpected action, sound or change. The two can overlap, but they are not identical. A
quiet food close-up can work as a visual opening without a sudden surprise. An unexpected
sound can be a pattern interrupt without explaining the subject visually.
Choose the approach that serves the topic. You do not need to add a dramatic zoom to every
reel. A clear image of the result may provide a better introduction to a careful demonstration.
Use the timing guide sensibly
The course treats the first roughly three seconds as a creative planning window, not a platform
rule. Remove blank frames and long logo animations before the subject appears. Start with the
relevant image and add introductions only when they help the viewer.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 4, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 07  /  PLAN, SHOOT AND CHECK
Visual Hooks: Make the First Frame Count
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
A practical planning sequence
1. Define the content first. Write what the reel will actually demonstrate: a recipe step,
product feature or styling idea. This is the payoff that the opening must support.
2. Choose one visual focus. Select a detail or action that represents that payoff. Decide
whether a close-up, movement or unusual angle makes it easiest to understand.
3. Frame and record the opening. Keep the subject visible and the background simple.
Record a clear beginning rather than adding a blank lead-in. Check focus and avoid motion that
hides the important detail.
4. Connect it to the next shot. Move directly into the promised explanation. Add a short text
overlay if the image needs context, then review the sequence both with sound and muted.
Illustrative English examples
- Food: open on steam rising from a freshly served bowl. Overlay: 'The final step in this soup.'
Payoff: show the actual finishing step and how it fits the recipe.
- Product: bring a customised stamp towards the lens, then reveal its printed impression.
Overlay: 'From this design to this print.' Payoff: demonstrate the same design and stamping
process.
- Fashion: begin with a close-up of a scarf knot, then widen to show the full look. Overlay: 'One
scarf, a simple knot.' Payoff: demonstrate the exact knot without switching to a different
result.
Common mistakes and fixes
If the opening is an abstract blur, give the object more space or reveal it sooner. If movement
feels distracting, slow or simplify it. If the text covers the detail, shorten or reposition it. If the
first image promises a result the reel never shows, change the opening or supply that missing
demonstration.
A visually unusual opening does not guarantee attention or reach. Judge it first on relevance,
legibility and whether the rest of the reel fulfils its promise.
Practice assignment
Plan three opening frames for your next topic: one close-up, one movement and one unusual
angle. Film the strongest option. Watch it muted and check that the subject is clear, no
introduction delays it, any overlay is readable and the next shot delivers a logical continuation.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 4, 6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: BUILD A USEFUL LIST
videos.description: Use numbered openings to communicate what a viewer can expect from your reel. Learn to choose a focused benefit, organise distinct points and keep the list manageable. This lesson also explains how to build towards a strong final point while delivering useful information throughout, supported by examples and a practical planning exercise.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 08  /  BUILD A USEFUL LIST
List Hooks: Turn a Number into a Clear
Promise
Structure a short list around a specific benefit and deliver every promised point.
What a number tells the viewer
A list hook names a number and a specific kind of value. Instead of introducing a broad topic
such as studying or content creation, it promises a defined set of ideas, mistakes, steps or tools.
The number helps the viewer understand the structure before the explanation begins.
The benefit must be as clear as the count. 'Three tips' gives little context; 'Three checks before
filming a product demo' tells a specific audience what the reel contains. A number organises
your promise, but it does not make weak, repetitive or unsupported advice useful.
The list-hook formula
The course recommends practising with three to five points. Treat this as a manageable writing
guide, not a platform limit. Choose the number after selecting useful content; do not inflate the
count by splitting one idea into several near-identical items.
The final point can provide a satisfying conclusion, but calling it 'the most important' requires an
honest reason. It might combine the earlier ideas or address the most consequential mistake in
your particular example. If all points are equally useful, introduce them plainly without inventing
a ranking.
LIST HOOK FORMULA
Number + specific topic or benefit + a clear reason to follow the list. Deliver the promised
number of distinct points, with a strong final point when the content supports that order.
Give value throughout the reel
Each item should add something new. Explain the point, show a quick example and move on.
Avoid delaying all useful information until the ending or repeatedly asking the viewer to wait. A
strong final item should reward attention after several useful points have already been
delivered.
A simple structure is opening promise, point one, point two, point three and a brief conclusion. A
visible number or short label can help the viewer follow the sequence. The visual should
demonstrate the item whenever possible instead of showing unrelated footage.
Keep the opening concise
Say the count and benefit early, and begin the first point promptly. The course's roughly
three-second opening target is a creative guide, not a rule imposed by a platform. If the
sentence is crowded, remove exaggerated adjectives and unnecessary setup before cutting
useful context.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 4-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 08  /  WRITE AND DELIVER THE PAYOFF
List Hooks: Turn a Number into a Clear Promise
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Plan the list step by step
1. Choose one audience and task. Name who the reel helps and what they are trying to do. A
narrow situation gives you a clearer list than a broad subject alone.
2. Select three to five distinct points. Write one sentence for each. Remove duplicates and
anything you cannot explain or demonstrate honestly within the planned reel.
3. Arrange the sequence. Put the points in a useful order, such as preparation, action and
final check. Reserve a strong conclusion only when it naturally follows from the other items.
4. Write the opening and visuals. State the number and benefit. Plan one relevant shot per
point and check that the completed reel delivers exactly what its opening promises.
Illustrative English examples
- Creator: 'Three checks before recording your voiceover.' Opening visual: a microphone beside
a short checklist. Payoff: show room noise, microphone position and a test recording; the final
check brings the earlier choices together.
- Student: 'Three things I prepare before a revision session.' Opening visual: a cluttered desk
becoming ready for work. Payoff: demonstrate the topic plan, necessary materials and a short
practice task, with one visible example of each item.
- Product business: 'Three shots that show this stamp clearly.' Opening visual: the product
beside its printed impression. Payoff: show the whole stamp, a close-up of the design and a
complete stamping demonstration.
Common mistakes and fixes
A long list can become rushed when every point needs explanation. Reduce the count or split
the topic into separate reels. If points overlap, combine them. If an item is only a vague slogan,
add a concrete demonstration or remove it.
Do not promise five items and deliver four, or repeat 'wait for the last one' instead of teaching.
Make the count match the finished edit. If the last item is not demonstrably stronger, remove
that claim and let the useful sequence carry the reel.
Practice assignment and review
Plan one list reel with a clear audience, numbered opening and three to five points. For each
point, write its explanation and matching visual. Confirm that every item is distinct, useful and
delivered, the opening works with a readable overlay, and the ending completes the promised
list without an unsupported claim.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 4-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: FIND THE RECOGNISABLE MOMENT
videos.description: Create relatable openings by turning specific audience experiences into short POV scenes. Learn to identify everyday situations, choose recognisable details and coordinate on-screen text with acting and visuals. The lesson covers common mistakes, practical examples and an exercise for developing relevant hooks without relying on vague captions or exaggerated promises.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 09  /  FIND THE RECOGNISABLE MOMENT
POV Hooks: Make a Familiar Situation
Specific
Use a recognisable everyday moment to introduce a scene your audience understands.
What POV means in this lesson
POV stands for point of view. In this course, a POV hook introduces a familiar situation with a
short 'POV:' caption and then acts out the moment. The viewer is invited to recognise an
experience, reaction or routine that feels relevant to their own life.
The format is more than placing those three letters over any video. The caption needs a specific
situation, and the visual needs to show it. A person looking surprised beneath the words 'POV:
life is hard' gives very little context. A visible task, meaningful detail and clear reaction make the
scene easier to understand.
The POV-hook formula
Start with an audience you understand: students revising, office workers finishing a task or
creators checking an edit. Choose an ordinary experience that has a clear emotional turn, such
as expecting to finish and discovering one more job.
Specificity comes from relevant details, not a longer sentence. A time, task, object or
interruption can make the scene recognisable. Include only what helps the intended audience
understand it. A moment familiar to your viewers can be effective without being universal.
POV HOOK FORMULA
POV: + a specific audience situation + a recognisable moment or reaction. Show the situation
immediately, then develop the joke, observation or useful response promised by the opening.
Act the situation rather than labelling it
Plan what the audience sees first: an open textbook, a nearly closed laptop or an editing
timeline. Then decide the smallest action that communicates the change, such as reopening the
book, pausing before leaving or spotting a misspelled caption.
The expression, prop and caption should describe the same event. Keep the action readable
with the sound off, and use speech only when it adds something. You can show an exaggerated
reaction for a clearly acted skit, but avoid presenting an invented experience as a factual
personal case study.
What the format can and cannot promise
A relatable scene may give viewers a reason to keep watching, but it does not guarantee shares,
comments or views. Review the match between your audience and situation first. The course's
opening timing guidance is a creative prompt to get to the moment quickly, not a fixed platform
requirement.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 09  /  WRITE, ACT AND REFINE
POV Hooks: Make a Familiar Situation Specific
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
A repeatable planning method
1. List real audience routines. Write five tasks or moments your viewers encounter. Use your
own relevant experience or what the audience actually tells you instead of assuming everyone
has the same problems.
2. Find the small tension. Identify what changes in each moment: a plan meets an
interruption, an expectation meets reality or a small mistake becomes visible. Keep it
understandable without a long explanation.
3. Write the POV line. Name the situation in one short sentence. Replace generic wording with
one detail that matters to that audience, then remove anything the picture already explains.
4. Plan the scene and payoff. Choose the opening prop, action and reaction. Decide how the
reel resolves the moment through a joke, observation or practical response. Film and review the
caption and action together.
Illustrative English examples
- Student skit: 'POV: you open tomorrow's revision checklist for the first time.' Opening visual: a
long checklist beside an untouched notebook. Payoff: the character reacts, then chooses one
section to begin; the scene delivers the stated situation.
- Office skit: 'POV: your laptop is closing when the last request arrives.' Opening visual: a hand
stopping the lid beside a clearly staged work message. Payoff: show the recognisable pause
and decision, then reopen the laptop to complete the final task.
- Creator skit: 'POV: you export the reel and then spot the typo.' Opening visual: a completed
export beside a visibly misspelled caption. Payoff: the creator catches the error and returns to
correct that caption.
Common mistakes and fixes
If the scene feels like a generic meme, replace the broad caption with a specific routine and
meaningful prop. If viewers need several sentences of explanation, simplify the situation. If the
caption describes one event but the acting shows another, revise them together.
Avoid stacking several unrelated frustrations into one short opening. Choose one moment and
let the reaction develop. Relevance matters more than making the situation louder or more
dramatic.
Practice assignment
Write five everyday moments for your audience and turn each into a POV hook. For every option,
add the first visible action and the intended payoff. Film one. Check that the caption is readable,
the scene makes sense muted and the ending develops the exact situation introduced.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 2-5.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

videos.title: CHOOSE AND COMBINE YOUR APPROACH
videos.description: Bring the eight hook types together in a practical content workflow. Learn to combine complementary approaches, brief ChatGPT for relevant options and compare openings before filming. The lesson introduces practical testing and review, then concludes with a final project: write one hook of each type and produce eight reels that fulfil their promises.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 10  /  CHOOSE AND COMBINE YOUR APPROACH
Your Hook Formula: Combine, Draft and
Test
Choose suitable hook types, use ChatGPT thoughtfully and improve through practical observation.
The principle that connects every hook
A hook is a promise made by the first line and visual. Choose it from your audience, topic and
intended payoff. No single type fits every reel; the eight approaches below give you different ways
to introduce that promise.
Hook typeCore approach
Curiosity gapOpen a specific question and deliver its answer.
Pattern interruptIntroduce a relevant unexpected action, sound or change.
Bold statementChallenge familiar advice with an honest explanation.
QuestionAsk about a specific audience problem.
StoryBegin at an interesting moment with brief context.
VisualLead with a meaningful close-up, movement or angle.
ListPromise a defined number of useful points.
POVAct a recognisable, specific everyday situation.
Combine two types for one clear purpose
Combine approaches that support the same promise. A visual can show the problem a question
names, or a story can introduce an unanswered question. Keep the opening focused on one idea.
- Question + visual: 'Why is this stamp print patchy?' Opening visual: a clear imperfect impression.
Payoff: demonstrate the actual cause and correction in your example.
- Story + curiosity: 'I was ready to export when I noticed this caption.' Opening visual: the editing
preview. Payoff: reveal the real error and show how you corrected it; use the personal claim only
if it happened.
Brief ChatGPT with useful constraints
Give ChatGPT the audience, topic, hook type and promised payoff. Use its suggestions as drafts;
choose natural wording and check that the claim matches your footage.
COMPLETE ENGLISH DRAFTING PROMPT
My niche: [niche]. My audience: [specific viewers]. Reel topic: [topic]. Hook type: [type or
two-type combination]. What my reel can honestly deliver: [payoff]. Write 10 distinct hook
options in natural English, each 1-2 lines. For each, include one sentence describing the opening
frame and the specific promise the reel must fulfil. Avoid invented facts, exaggerated results
and claims of guaranteed engagement. Aim for an opening line that takes roughly three
seconds to say naturally.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES1 / 2

SKILLOMATEVIRAL HOOK FORMULA
LESSON 10  /  COMPARE, OBSERVE AND COMPLETE THE PROJECT
Your Hook Formula: Combine, Draft and Test
Detailed lesson notes | Practice, checks and application
Compare two drafts before filming
Select two hooks for the same topic and payoff. Score each from 1-10 for clarity, attention
potential and whether its promise can be delivered. Explain each score using the wording and
planned visual. These scores are editorial judgements, not measured performance or predictions
of views.
Use this prompt: 'Compare hook A: [A] and hook B: [B] for [audience], with this payoff: [payoff].
Score clarity, attention potential and deliverability from 1-10. Explain the trade-offs, identify
unsupported promises and improve the clearer option without adding claims.'
Run a practical comparison carefully
1. Change the opening. Prepare two versions with different hooks and the same main
content, payoff and overall structure. Keep other controllable choices similar so the opening is
the main planned difference.
2. Record the conditions. Note what changed and how each version was shared. Similar
publishing conditions are useful, but separate posts may reach different people; this is practical
observation, not a fully controlled experiment.
3. Review appropriate measures. Where available, compare early retention or
viewer-continuation rates at the same point, using the same metric definition. Record the
sample size and inspect whether viewers stay for the payoff. Raw view totals alone cannot
isolate the hook's effect.
4. Repeat and refine. Look for patterns across several comparable topics. A single pair does
not prove one formula always wins. Use observations to improve the next opening while
checking the quality of the full reel.
Final project: eight hooks, eight reels
Write one hook for each of the eight types in your niche, then shoot eight reels that deliver those
promises. For each, save the hook, opening-frame plan, intended payoff and finished reel.
Review your choices and identify one improvement to try next.
Final publishing check
- The opening is concise, specific and free of a delayed logo or blank introduction.
- The first visual and readable overlay support understanding without sound.
- Every statement is honest, and the reel delivers the promised answer or demonstration.
Sources: Course Notes pp. 1, 5-6; Chatbot Knowledge Base pp. 1-3, 5-6.
ENGLISH EDITION  |  STUDENT LESSON NOTES2 / 2

courses.title: AI Real Estate Videos
courses.description:
**AI Real Estate Videos — From Empty Rooms to Cinematic Property Reels**

Learn how to transform property photographs into professional-looking real estate videos using AI. This practical course takes you through property planning, virtual staging, realistic lighting enhancements, AI-powered walkthroughs, cinematic montages, and final reel editing.

Work with ChatGPT, Google Flow, Nano Banana Pro, and CapCut to create engaging property presentations while preserving original layouts, architectural details, and authentic views.

You'll also learn how to package these skills into a creative service for real estate brokers and builders, with an emphasis on transparent AI disclosures and honest property representation.

videos.title: Course Introduction
videos.description: Discover how AI can transform ordinary property photographs into cinematic listing videos. Understand the complete production workflow, explore the tools used throughout the course, and learn the importance of maintaining accurate property representation.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 01 - Course Introduction
Learning outcome: Understand the complete workflow for turning authentic property photos into an
AI-assisted listing reel, while distinguishing visualization from the actual property.
The end-to-end production workflow
Begin with a real property or clearly labeled practice images. Collect the property facts and photos, prepare a
listing brief and shot list, write Room Lock constraints, stage selected rooms, create alternate lighting, animate
still images, assemble cinematic clips, and finish the listing reel in CapCut. This sequence matters because
each later step should inherit verified information and visual references from earlier work.
What each tool does
ChatGPT organizes the property brief, shot list, Room Lock descriptions, image/video prompts, captions and
service materials. Google Flow uses Nano Banana Pro for still-image work and Frames mode for video clips.
CapCut is used to arrange the clips, add text and disclosures, and export the finished vertical reel.
Practice versus client work
The course demonstrates a sample 2BHK flat in Vijay Nagar, Indore, using AI-generated sample images.
Those images are practice material, not evidence of a real listing. Client deliverables should be based on the
actual property and verified information supplied with permission.
Truthful visualization
Virtual staging may illustrate furniture and decor, but it must not misrepresent structural details or amenities.
Every AI-staged photo or video must carry a visible "Virtually Staged" label. Do not present AI-generated
scenes as genuine camera footage.
First assignment
Photograph four or five views of a room or property you can legitimately use. Keep the originals. Record which
details are confirmed and which are unknown. These will become the reference material for the next lesson.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.

videos.title: Property Planning: Brief, Shot List
videos.description: Learn how to turn verified property information into a structured creative plan. Create professional property briefs, organize video shot lists, and develop Room Lock instructions that preserve architectural details throughout AI generation.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 02 - Property Planning: Brief, Shot List
and Room Lock
Learning outcome: Build a factual property brief and a practical reel plan before generating visuals.
Create the property brief
Record BHK, floor, location, approximate area, actual highlights and intended buyer. The course sample is a
third-floor, approximately 1,100 sq ft 2BHK in Vijay Nagar, Indore, with an east-facing balcony, modular
kitchen, sunlight, parking and lift. These are sample details only; replace them with verified client information.
Turn the brief into a shot list
Plan a 30-40 second vertical reel from the exterior toward the balcony. For each shot identify room, visible
subject, one camera move, mood or lighting and duration. Keep individual shots to eight seconds or less. If
there is no authentic image of an advertised feature, omit that shot rather than inventing the image.
Write a Room Lock for every photograph
A Room Lock describes the features that AI must preserve: walls, window size and position, doors, flooring,
ceiling, apparent room dimensions and camera angle. Write a separate English line for each image, based on
what is actually visible. The same line is reused in later staging, lighting and video prompts.
Check for contradictions
Compare the brief against the photos. A listed lift or parking space does not justify showing it if there is no valid
visual reference. Do not assume a room is larger or that the balcony has a better view than the supplied
photograph shows.
Practical assignment
Produce one verified property brief, one shot-list table and one Room Lock per available image. Save them
together so the following lessons use a consistent reference.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.

- Location: Vijay Nagar, Indore
- Size: approx 1100 sq ft
- Highlights: east-facing balcony, modular kitchen, achhi sunlight, society mein parking
aur lift
- Buyer: young working couple ya chhoti family
Is property ka ek short listing brief banao — main selling points, kis buyer ke liye best
hai, aur reel ka mood kya hona chahiye. Koi feature apni taraf se mat jodna, sirf jo maine
bataya.
Message 2: Shot list
Ab is property ki 30–40 second ki vertical listing reel ka shot list banao. Har shot ke
liye table do: shot number, room, kya dikhana hai, camera move (jaise slow push-in, side
glide), mood/lighting, aur kitne seconds. Exterior se shuru karo aur balcony pe end karo.
Har shot 8 second ya kam ka ho.
Message 3: Room Lock (saari photos upload karke)
Ye is property ki photos hain. Har photo ke liye ek "Room Lock" line likho — us room ki
woh cheezein jo AI editing mein KABHI change nahi honi chahiye: walls, windows ki position

videos.title: Virtual Staging
videos.description: Transform empty rooms into beautifully furnished interiors using AI-powered virtual staging. Explore different interior styles, write precise prompts, maintain realistic furniture proportions, and prevent unwanted changes to the original room.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 03 - Virtual Staging
Learning outcome: Add realistic furniture and decor to existing rooms without changing the actual
property.
Start from the exact original room
Upload the empty-room photo as the image reference in Google Flow to Image to Nano Banana Pro. The
course instructs prompts to begin: "Use the attached photo as the exact room. Only add furniture and decor -
do not change anything else." Follow it with the room-specific Room Lock.
Modern Indian styling
For the living room and master bedroom, use warm wood, beige and off-white fabrics, one indoor plant and soft
warm lighting. Keep furniture proportions believable for the actual room; preserve the camera angle and
ordinary smartphone-photo appearance.
Create a controlled alternative
Generate a second living-room option using minimal Scandinavian styling: light oak, white and grey, and clean,
simple furniture. Change the styling only; do not change walls, openings, floors or camera perspective.
Inspect before and after
Place the original and staged images side by side. Check window placement, floor pattern, doorway, ceiling
and room proportions. Reject any output that makes the room look structurally different or deceptively larger.
Common failure and correction
The deliberately weak example "Furnish this room nicely" gives the model too much freedom and may alter the
structure. Correct it with the original reference, explicit furniture-only instruction and exact Room Lock.
Practical assignment
Stage one empty room in two distinct styles, preserve the original photo, and note any differences that would
make the staging unsuitable for a real listing.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.

not change anything else."
- Us room ki Room Lock line jo tumne pehle likhi thi, word-to-word
- Style: modern Indian home — warm wood, beige aur off-white fabrics, ek indoor plant,
soft warm lighting
- Furniture ka size room ke hisaab se realistic ho, room bada ya chhota na dikhe

videos.title: Lighting Upgrade: Day to Evening
videos.description: Create appealing golden-hour and evening variations of property photographs. Learn to enhance lighting, atmosphere, and presentation while preserving the original surroundings, architectural features, and exterior views.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 04 - Lighting Upgrade: Day to Evening
Learning outcome: Create golden-hour and evening looks while preserving the real building and exterior
views.
Three lighting scenarios
The course covers a building exterior at golden hour, a staged living room with warm evening lights and a
balcony at sunset. Use the correct image reference for each; the living room should use the previously staged
image.
Constrain the transformation
Begin with: "Use the attached photo as the exact scene. Only change the lighting and time of day - do not
change anything else." Add the appropriate Room Lock. Preserve buildings, trees, cars, roads, furniture and
exterior view.
Make light changes plausible
Describe the warmer sky or indoor lamp illumination while retaining the original physical scene. The goal is to
show a lighting visualization, not to imply a different neighborhood, larger windows or amenities that do not
exist.
Failure example
The vague instruction "make it look beautiful at night" changed the surrounding road and cars in the course
demonstration. Use explicit scene-preservation instructions and compare every major background landmark
with the original.
Practical assignment
Generate exterior, staged-living-room and balcony evening variants. Review each against its source and label
staged or AI-altered material clearly in any client-facing use.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.

Message 1: Light upgrade prompts (ChatGPT)
Ab light upgrade karna hai. Google Flow (Nano Banana Pro) ke liye 3 image prompts likho,
main har baar wali photo reference mein upload karunga:
1. Building exterior — golden hour evening: warm sunset light, soft orange-pink sky,
balconies aur windows ki lights on
2. Staged living room (modern Indian wala) — evening look: lamps aur ceiling lights on,
warm cozy light, window ke bahar halki sham
3. Balcony — sunset look: warm golden light floor aur railing par
Har prompt mein:
- Pehli line: "Use the attached photo as the exact scene. Only change the lighting and
time of day — do not change anything else."
- Us photo ki Room Lock line word-to-word (exterior, living room, balcony)
- Bahar ka view, buildings, trees, furniture — sab same rahe. Koi naya view, pool, garden
ya extra cheez add nahi karni
- Same camera angle, same phone-photo look, no people, no text
Teeno prompts English mein, copy-paste ready.

videos.title: Walkthrough Video
videos.description: Bring static property photographs to life using Google Flow's video generation tools. Learn to create smooth camera movements, realistic walkthrough clips, and day-to-evening transitions while maintaining visual consistency.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 05 - Walkthrough Video
Learning outcome: Animate reference photographs into controlled vertical walkthrough clips using
Google Flow Frames mode.
Set up Frames mode
Use Google Flow to Video to Frames. Set a 9:16 output and an eight-second duration, with the appropriate
property photo as the start frame. The course demonstrates a building push-in, living-room side glide, bedroom
pan and balcony push-in.
One movement per shot
Keep each clip to a single simple, slow camera move. Include the instruction: "Only the camera moves. The
room, furniture, walls, windows and view stay exactly the same." Avoid adding people, objects, text or music
within the generated clip.
Day-to-evening transition
Use the daylight living-room image as the start frame and the evening variant as the end frame. Keep the
camera stationary and describe the gradual change in light. Both frames must depict the same room geometry
and furnishings.
Troubleshooting invented spaces
The weak prompt "camera flies through the whole house fast" can create corridors or rooms that are not
present. Return to a short movement, reference frame and explicit room preservation. Review every generated
frame for morphing.
Practical assignment
Generate at least three short walkthrough clips and one day-to-evening experiment. Record which camera
movements maintained the original layout.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.
videos.examplePrompt:
Galti wala prompt (Flow Video, sirf comparison ke liye)
camera flies through the whole house fast
Message 1: Walkthrough + day-to-evening prompts (ChatGPT)
Ab walkthrough video banana hai. Apni shot list ke hisaab se Google Flow Video (Frames
mode, start frame = photo) ke liye 4 video prompts likho, 9:16, 8 seconds:
1. Building exterior (golden evening wali photo) — slow push-in toward the building
2. Living room (modern Indian staged, din wali) — slow smooth glide from left to right
3. Master bedroom (staged) — slow pan across the room
4. Balcony (sunset wali) — slow push-in toward the railing and the view
Har prompt mein:
- "Only the camera moves. The room, furniture, walls, windows and view stay exactly the
same."
- Ek hi simple, slow camera move — koi fast move ya 360 nahi
- No people, no new objects, no text, no music
- Real phone-video jaisa natural look
Ek 5th prompt bhi do: living room ka day-to-evening transition — start frame din wali
photo, end frame evening wali photo, camera static, lights dheere-dheere on hoti hain.
Saare prompts English mein, copy-paste ready.

videos.title: Cinematic Montage
videos.description: Take your property videos further with dynamic camera movements and high-energy cinematic sequences. Create FPV-style shots, dramatic close-ups, and fast montages while keeping the property visually accurate.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 06 - Cinematic Montage
Learning outcome: Build a fast, high-energy property montage from short clips without fabricating the
property.
Design the shot sequence
The course proposes five four-second shots: exterior FPV rise, low-angle living-room push-in, living-room
macro pull-back, bedroom whip-pan half-arc and balcony FPV push toward the actual view.
Use fast motion carefully
Each shot should have one clearly described aggressive camera move, with motion blur during speed and a
sharp final frame. Use the original or staged source photograph as the start frame in Flow Frames mode, with
the corresponding Room Lock.
Maintain the property lock
Explicitly preserve the room, furniture, walls, windows and outside view. Do not add rooms, amenities, furniture
or landscapes. High-energy camera movement is a visual technique, not permission to invent a new property.
Assemble in Flow
Generate the clips, open a clip as a scene, then use Add clip to order the montage from exterior to interior and
finally balcony. Check that visual continuity survives the transitions.
Fix slow or distorted results
If the result is too slow, rewrite the prompt with a clearer camera move and speed description. If the room
morphs, shorten the shot and remove simultaneous moves rather than relaxing the Room Lock.
Practical assignment
Create five short clips and assemble a single montage. Review both visual energy and accuracy of the
depicted property.
Course reference and integrity
These expanded notes are based on the supplied Course Notes, Chatbot Knowledge Base and All Prompts documents.
The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.
videos.examplePrompt:
Message 1: Fast montage prompts (ChatGPT)
Ab is property ka ek FAST, high-energy cinematic montage banana hai — jaise luxury
property trailers aur viral Instagram real-estate reels mein hota hai. Aise shots jo phone
se shoot hi nahi ho sakte.
Google Flow Video (Frames mode, start frame = meri photo) ke liye 5 prompts likho, 9:16, 4
seconds each:
1. Building exterior (golden evening) — fast FPV drone rise from street level up the
building facade
2. Living room (modern Indian staged, evening) — rapid low-angle push-in toward the sofa,
almost touching the floor
3. Living room detail — extreme close-up macro on the lamp and coffee table, then fast
pull-back reveal of the room
4. Master bedroom (staged) — quick whip pan into a fast half-arc around the bed
5. Balcony (sunset) — fast FPV push through the balcony door straight to the railing,
ending on the real view
Har prompt mein:
- Camera speed FAST aur aggressive, speed-ramp feel (fast start, slow-motion end), motion
blur on the fast part, crisp sharp frame at the end
- Har clip mein sirf EK fast move — taaki room morph na ho
- Us photo ki Room Lock line word-to-word
- "The room, furniture, walls, windows and outside view stay exactly the same. Do not add
any new rooms, objects, views or amenities."
- Look: high-end cinematic real-estate film, punchy contrast, no people, no text, no music
Har prompt ke start mein camera move ek line mein likho (jaise "FAST FPV DRONE RISE").
Saare prompts English mein, copy-paste ready.

videos.title: Final Listing Reel
videos.description: Combine your AI-generated clips into a polished vertical property reel using CapCut. Learn video sequencing, on-screen text, captions, music selection, export settings, and proper virtual-staging disclosures.
videos.notes:
SKILLOMATE  |  AI REAL ESTATE VIDEOS1
SKILLOMATE / COURSE NOTES
Lesson 07 - Final Listing Reel
Learning outcome: Assemble the final vertical listing reel with verified text, clear disclosure and a
professional export.
Plan the finished edit
The course targets a 20-25 second, 9:16 listing reel in CapCut. Import the clips, lead with the cinematic
montage, and then add the day-to-evening sequence where appropriate. Maintain a clear visual progression.
Write concise on-screen text
Use five or six short lines of no more than five words each. Cover the hook, verified location, size/BHK, two
confirmed highlights and an end card. Use "Price on request" rather than inventing a sale price.
Disclose visual staging
Show a visible "Virtually Staged" label on AI-staged clips. Include a readable end-card statement: "Virtually
Staged - furniture and decor are digitally added for visualization." Never describe AI-generated video as
genuine camera footage.
Prepare caption and sound
Create a short Hinglish Instagram caption, eight relevant hashtags and a music mood such as energetic, luxury
or chill. The caption must reflect verified facts; do not add a pool, view, size or amenity not supplied by the
client.
Export and inspect
Export at 1080p in 9:16. Watch the entire reel to check text legibility, disclosure visibility, shot order and any
accidental misrepresentation.
Practical assignment
Complete one final reel and accompanying caption, then perform a factual accuracy and disclosure checklist
before sharing.
Course reference and integrity

The Indore flat is a sample scenario, not a verified listing. Exact copy-paste prompt wording is maintained in the original All
Prompts document; use that document when verbatim reproduction is required.

location, size/BHK, 2 highlights, aur end card. Sirf wahi details jo maine brief mein di

2. Ek line ka "Virtually Staged" disclaimer jo staged clips par dikhega.
3. Instagram caption (Hinglish, 3–4 lines) + 8 relevant hashtags.
4. Music ka mood — kis type ka track lagaun (energetic / luxury / chill).
Simple rakho, cheesy mat banana.
